speechtext:
One year ago today, on July 23, 1962, an international agreement on the Laotian question was signed at Geneva. The 13 governments whose representatives signed that agreement solemnly declared that they would "respect and observe in every way the sovereignty, independence, neutrality, unity and territorial integrity" of the kingdom of Laos.
Unfortunately during the past year there has not been much progress in that direction. The administration and armed forces of Laos have not been integrated. The country remains divided and there has been a renewal, on a limited scale, of fighting. The international commission of which Canada, India and Poland are members, has not been allowed to circulate freely through the country in order to supervise the implementation of the agreement.
However, the international commission has made a number of limited investigations and on May 17, 1963, three majority reports were submitted by the Canadian and Indian commissioners, the Polish commissioner having declined to associate himself with them. In accordance with the Geneva protocol these reports are strictly factual, but from a reading of them it is quite clear that the Pathet Lao and their dissident neutralist allies are responsible for the recent deterioration of the situation in Laos.
I wish to table copies of these three reports numbered 22, 23 and 24. Canada will of course continue, as a member of the commission, to strive for Laotian unity and neutrality, the objectives of the Geneva agreement of 1962.

Nationals from other countries are still fishing within the 12 mile limit off Canada's coasts. Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question of the hon. gentleman I think it is inaccurate to use the words "to free the ship", because this ship is not imprisoned in the port of Chicago. It is true that the ship has gone there to be loaded and that the union has refused to load it.
As the hon. gentleman may know, as a result of what I consider to be extraordinary assistance from the justice department and the labour department of the United States, the Chicago court did issue an injunction which would have had the effect of ordering the affected union members to load the ship. However, the fact is that the union members refused to obey the injunction, and about three weeks ago, as a further legal step, the national labour relations board attempted to lay the foundation for contempt proceedings against the union members. The Canadian government has made quite frequent representations to the United States authorities and has sought the co-operation of these authorities, particularly with respect to the port situation in Chicago, which is very difficult. 1.	That with respect to new depreciable property of a prescribed class acquired in the period of 24 months commencing June 14, 1963 capital cost allowances be computed on a straight line basis at a prescribed rate not exceeding 50 per cent per annum if the property has been acquired by a taxpayer in a taxation year for a manufacturing or processing business in Canada and the taxpayer is
(a)	an individual who was resident in Canada for a period of not less than 183 days in the year, or
(b)	a corporation that in the year had a degree of Canadian ownership and control;
and for the purposes of this paragraph,
(c)	a corporation has a degree of Canadian ownership and control in a year if the corporation throughout the 60 day period immediately preceding the year (or if the corporation did not have a preceding year, throughout the 60 day period commencing on the first day of the year) complied with the following conditions:
(i)	the corporation was resident in Canada,
(ii)	either
(A)	not less than 25 per cent of its voting shares were beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, one or more corporations controlled in Canada or a combination thereof,
or
(B)	the voting shares of the corporation were listed on a recognized stock exchange in Canada and it is established, in prescribed manner, that no one non-resident shareholder owned beneficially, together with any other person associated with

him at any time in the period, more than 75 per cent of the voting shares of the corporation, and
(iii)	where the year commences after December 31, 1964, the number of directors of the corporation who were resident in Canada was not less than 25 per cent of the total number of directors of the corporation;
or complied with the conditions specified in clauses (i) and (iii) and was a wholly-owned subsidiary of a corporation that throughout the 60 day period complied with the conditions specified in clauses (i), (ii) and (iii); and
(d)	a corporation is controlled in Canada at a particular time if at that time it complies with the following conditions:
(i)	the corporation is resident in Canada, and
(ii)	not less than 51 per cent of its voting shares are beneficially owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada, one or more corporations controlled in Canada or a combination thereof.
2.	That a taxpayer whose business in a prescribed area of Canada has been certified to be a new manufacturing or processing business that commenced commercial operations in the period of 24 months commencing with the date on which any enactment based on this paragraph is assented to be exempt from tax on the income from that business for a period of 36 months from the date certified to be the date of commencement of operations, and that the rate of capital cost allowances for new depreciable property of a prescribed class acquired by the said taxpayer in the said 24 months period for such business be computed on a straight line basis at a prescribed rate not exceeding 50 per cent per annum.
3.	That with effect for 1964 and subsequent taxation years section 40A of the act, which provides for a deduction from the tax otherwise payable by a manufacturing and processing corporation, be repealed.

That with respect to expenses incurred after June 13, 1963 a corporation whose principal business is operating a pipe line for the transmission of oil or natural gas be allowed to deduct in computing income the drilling and exploration expenses, including all general geological and geophysical expenses, incurred by it on or in respect of exploring for petroleum or natural gas in Canada and the prospecting, exploration and development expenses incurred by it in searching for minerals in Canada.

(a)	5 per cent of any dividends paid or credited by the corporation to him after June 13, 1963 and before January 1, 1965, in respect of which he has paid a tax of 15 per cent to Canada, and

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this paragraph of the resolution proposes that a taxpayer who is dissatisfied with the direction of the minister in connection with dividend stripping or associated companies may appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I spoke at some length on this matter when we were dealing with the budget speech per se, and I do not intend to repeat now what I said on that occasion.
Hear, hear.

Well, if there is to be noise over there I will. I think the minister has attempted to improve the situation by the insertion of this appeal section, but I doubt very much that it achieves the purpose. As was pointed out by other members in the discussion last night, I do not think any appeal provision will meet the situation. However, I think the proper thing to do is to wait until the bill is before us, when we will have the various sections of the bill rather than spending considerable time in dealing with resolutions which, although important, are not effective in the same way that clauses of a bill are. So as far as we are concerned I think we are prepared to let the matter stand until we see the bill.

In preparing the bill I wonder whether the minister would be willing to consider that the appeal should start at the tax appeal board level rather than in the exchequer court. The provision here is a specific one for an appeal to the exchequer

court rather than to the tax appeal board and so far as many smaller taxpayers are concerned I think there might be a good deal of merit in allowing them at least to start with an appeal to the tax appeal board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there would be no objection to that, except that in the discussions it was felt that the tax appeal board was probably not in a position to deal with these matters as expeditiously or perhaps as fully as the exchequer court. However, I would be glad to consider the matter and look into it more carefully between now and the introduction of the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we proceed to the consideration of paragraph 19?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is another section that is designed to plug a loophole. It is an amendment to stop a device whereby a company that has experienced a loss is purchased by somebody else for the purpose of applying the loss against income from another business.

Mr. Chairman, I fully understand the minister's thinking concerning the plugging of loopholes, but might not this first business be sold to another business for a quite legitimate reason? Is there any protection under those circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There might be occasions where this could happen. I think the hon. member will agree with me, though, that in the vast majority of cases, particularly in recent years, this practice, which has been an ever-increasing one, has been for the simple purpose of avoiding taxes in future for profitable concerns.

I do not agree entirely. I feel that because of succession duties and all sorts of things there have been many cases in the past where a corporation, even though it has suffered losses in the previous year, may be sold to some other concern which has every right to take the losses in the previous year of the first company into consideration. I just do not like to see us put in the position where this may be forbidden.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I should have explained that this only applies in a case where the first business has been discontinued. It does not apply if the business is a continuing one with some losses that can be applied in the future. It is restricted to a case where the corporation has gone out of business with heavy losses. There used to be a regular market for such corporations.
Income Tax Act

It should be clearly understood that when the legislation comes before the house the provision will be clearly identified. One can readily envisage the condition referred to by the hon. member for Perth, where you might have two related businesses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not intended to cover those at all.

Of course we are fully aware that there was some, shall we say, plucking of ripe plums from certain trees by people who were rather astute at picking up tax losses of one company to the benefit of another. On the other hand, this legislation might become far too wide. A successful merger might be made of one or two unsuccessful businesses with one that is quite successful, or there might be the gathering together of two or three rather rundown businesses with a view to putting them on their feet, as long as there was a certain amount of working capital that might be introduced by the fourth corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is fair to say that this would stop the most blatant cases, but there might be a more sophisticated situation of the kind the hon. member has just described that would probably get through the net.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we go to paragraph 20?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This paragraph of the resolution proposes that section 18 of the act which deals with lease operations be repealed. This is another major plugging of a loophole and one that has been taken advantage of to an increasing extent in recent years.
Briefly, section 18 provides that lease options or similar agreements under which the lessee has the right to purchase shall be deemed to be agreements for the sale of the property. The lessee is not permitted to deduct the rent he pays for the use of the property, but he may deduct the cost of capital allowance. The original purpose of this section was to block arrangements under which contractors were leasing equipment and paying a rental which was sufficient to pay for the equipment in two or three years, after which the contractor had the right to buy the equipment for a nominal sum. This had the effect of allowing the contractor to deduct the cost of the equipment under the guise of rent over a very short period, and then write off the cost for tax purposes at a faster rate than would be allowed.

Oh, oh.

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I see the hon. member who for some years administered this act recognizes some of the cases to which I am referring. The contractor would then write off the cost at a faster rate than would be allowed under normal depreciation allowance for whatever equipment had been purchased.
In 1948 the section was rewritten and an attempt was made to prevent the purchase price of land being deducted under the heading of rental payments. It has been found that the section has a number of serious deficiencies, and it interferes with legitimate business transactions. On the other hand it provides a way for substantial tax avoidance. It is believed it would be extremely difficult to devise an amendment to correct the deficiencies of the section without interfering further with legitimate business arrangements and making an already difficult section incomprehensible. I do not think that is an exaggeration.
A brief submitted by a joint committee representing the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants for the last two years has urged repeal of the section.

I quite agree that there have been occasions when it might have been abused. The practice to which the minister has referred was a fairly ancient and shall I say honourable tradition. At any rate, it is one which has been in effect for a long while. I am particularly intrigued by the wording in one part. What does the minister mean by "appropriate transitional provision"? This is something I have not seen in resolutions heretofore, and I would hope that the section, when incorporated in the act, would translate "appropriate transitional provision" into a regulation which would enable us to know specifically with what we are dealing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the point that has been raised is a very good one. I will indicate, with the approval of the committee, three of the types of measures that are proposed. First of all, in those cases where rents already paid in previous years exceed capital cost allowances that have been deducted in those years, the excess of rents shall be deductible in the year first affected by the repeal of the section. Second, in those cases where the capital cost allowances deducted have exceeded the amount paid in rents, the excess shall be recovered by adding it to income. The taxpayer should be given the right to elect to spread this additional income over the previous five years in accordance with section 43.
Third, where the financing of ships built in Canada has been facilitated by an agreement under section 18, no recapture along

the lines indicated is required, and instead, any subsequent payment of rent, charter party fees, shall not be deducted until the total of such rentals exceeds the capital cost allowance. The final adjustment shall be made at the termination of the agreement.

This may be a rather technical point. I take it that the provision for spreading the recapture over the previous five years does not in fact open up the assessment in the fifth year so there can be a full reassessment which goes beyond the four year statutory limitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that the significance of that question has escaped my officials. Perhaps the hon. member would be kind enough to repeat it?

I am just worried that by spreading this recapture over five years, by going into the last year, the furthest year, you are in effect having a reassessment, and by so doing even at the option of the taxpayer you may be reopening an assessment that had been closed beyond the statutory period.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This would only be done at the option of the taxpayer. It is proposed that he have this option so that if he is stuck he can spread the additional cost over a reasonable period of years. Perhaps the hon. member would prefer to limit it to four years, but the intention is just to produce an average rate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We shall now proceed to paragraph 21.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This paragraph of the resolution provides that the present concession to exclude from the income tax of an employee certain benefits he receives from an employer through contributions to a group life insurance plan will be allowed only if the contributions are for term life insurance. That is to say that they would not be for permanent life insurance, because this may mean unduly large benefits for selected employees. This is just another loophole.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Paragraph 22.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This paragraph of the resolution proposes an amendment to ensure that interest earned on amounts paid to purchase an annuity contract will be taxed where proceeds of the contract are taken in a lump sum rather than in a life annuity. It is the same principle. This is another measure to close a loophole.
I take it that the time at which the income is computed by the recipient is when he receives the lump sum, and it will be deemed to be income within that taxation year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Paragraph 23.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This paragraph of the resolution proposes that a set of rules be added to the Income Tax Act to deal with certain taxation problems which arise when a person becomes bankrupt. At present it does not include special provisions governing a trustee of a bankrupt corporation or an individual, and as a result the trustee in bankruptcy must be taxed under the provisions of the law applicable to an estate or trust. This leaves uncovered a wide range of situations.
Moreover, if a trustee earns any income, and they often do, he would be taxed at the individual rates without exemptions, even when the bankrupt person is a corporation and frequently the trustee continues the operation. In the past, returns have been made and filed on assessment of what seems to be the most reasonable basis for handling the situation. However, the basis used has been questioned and there is need for more detailed law.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Have we completed discussion of paragraph 23?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then I should inform the committee that in the course of the discussion paragraphs 1, 6, 7, 8 and 9 were allowed to stand.

Mr. Chairman, this might be an appropriate moment to call to the attention of the committee what I consider to be some of the omissions in the resolution. We have been dealing at some length with provisions which affect corporate taxpayers, and according to the minister we have been attempting to plug some loopholes. Under other provisions we have been concerning ourselves with the granting of certain taxation concessions to corporate taxpayers, and it might be appropriate if we were to spend a little time concerning ourselves with matters relating to the far larger number of individual taxpayers. To my mind the resolution has some serious omissions in this connection.
In my experience during the time I have been in this house, this seems to have been an all too prevalent condition pertaining to the income tax resolutions and bills introduced by various ministers of finance, and the particular matter to which I make reference is certainly not new so far as I am concerned. I am sure the former minister of finance will
Income Tax Act
recall that during a somewhat similar discussion last year I raised a question in regard to limitations on exemptions of expenses incurred by individual taxpayers in the course of earning a living, because of the restrictions in section 5(2) of the Income Tax Act.
Perhaps the present minister may recall that last year I introduced an amendment in the committee stage of the bill which the chairman ruled out of order; and in spite of my plea to the then minister of finance that he accept my motion, and thereby put it in order, he indicated in a genial way that he did not see fit to adopt that suggestion. In passing I may say I have had a rather similar experience with quite a number of ministers of finance. I recall that when the first Conservative minister of finance of the current era in Canadian politics assumed office we had a similar discussion, and I remember saying at that time that apparently I was going to have to start all over again on a new minister of finance. I only hope that my starting on the present minister will be more effective than my previous experiences.
In this connection I would like to draw to the attention of the minister a statement which was made in this chamber by Mr. Harris, the then minister of finance, as recorded at page 3034 of Hansard, 1957, volume III. He was the last previous spokesman on behalf of a Liberal government in that portfolio, and on that occasion he had this to say:
The hon. member argues, in any event, that on social grounds it is desirable that full income tax should not be charged to men who are away from home because they ought to have a home life and be able to return and have some money with which to do it. I recognize both these arguments and I can assure hon. members that the subject is not closed.
It appears to have been closed during the period since 1957.
It is one of the problems to which we have to find a proper answer, but I am not prepared to make any recommendation to the committee at the present time.
In reply to that statement I had this to say, as recorded at page 3036 of Hansard:
I welcome the statement which the minister has made in part, because up until this year the only thing I have been able to get in the way of an answer from the opposite side of the house has been a few inconclusive words from the minister's parliamentary assistant on the subject. The one point to which I want to make reference, seeing that the discussion has gone this far, is this.
I agree in part with what the minister has been saying, namely that this problem is not something which is unique to the construction industry.
The present minister may recall that there was a great deal of discussion in respect to this sort of exemption being applicable to the construction industry. Following the taking of office by the Conservative administration, subsection 2 of section 5 of the act was

Income Tax Act
introduced, and it does provide some consideration for construction workers in respect to the deduction of expenses. In fact, as I recall the debate which occurred during that particular session, and from the records which I have been quoting, some of the then front bench members of the Conservative opposition dealt with the subject at considerable length, and I have always surmised that when shortly afterward they found themselves sitting on the treasury benches they could not do any more than show good faith in the course of action which they had been advocating so vigorously a short time previously.
The then minister of finance was trying to point out that this was not a problem confined only to the construction industry. As I was saying, in speaking at that time I said this:
I agree in part with what the minister has been saying, namely that this problem is not something which is unique to the construction industry. As far as I am concerned, it applies equally, and as seriously, for example to the logging industry. In my opinion from the study I have made of the matter over the past several sessions, this whole question can be resolved only by a suitable amendment to the Income Tax Act, one that will remove what to me is a discrimination that now exists against the expenses that are incurred by those on wages and salaries in the course of earning a living.
While no action has been taken by parliament in regard to legislation since the amendment covering construction workers was introduced by the Conservatives, this matter has not been allowed to lie dormant. I am not sure whether in the voluminous correspondence the Minister of Finance has been receiving in connection with budget matters he has had an opportunity of personally examining a brief which was submitted to him very recently, dated July 8 of this year, from what is referred to in British Columbia as the loggers' local of the international woodworkers of America. This particular brief merely reiterates the case that this local union, on behalf of its membership, has been placing before the minister of finance in Ottawa for quite a number of years.
While it is concerned primarily with the situation of the loggers on the Pacific coast, large numbers of whom have to spend most of their working life away from their homes and families and have to undertake expensive air travel as well as having to incur expenses for the special tools of their trade, nevertheless it is in line with the argument I have been attempting to present in the house and which was concurred in, in part at least, by the former minister of finance, Hon. Walter Harris, when I suggested that the only proper way to deal with this matter

was to provide the same rights of deduction for all people in the same or equivalent situations.
I am sure that people on wages and salaries in this country will have noted with interest the brave efforts of the present minister to curb what he termed expense account living; the suggestion that no one should be able to have a car valued at over $5,000, as I recall his figure, and write it off to expense. But I would urge that the minister consider that as long as any form of expense account living is allowed in this country, then under the same terms and conditions expenses incurred in the course of earning a living should be allowed to more Canadians no matter what the source of their income may happen to be.
It is for that reason, and in the hope that the present Minister of Finance will give a really sympathetic hearing to this argument that I have been presenting and perhaps agree that this should be incorporated in his proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act, that I would like to move:
That the resolution be amended by adding thereto after item 23 the following:
24.	That for the 1962 and subsequent taxation years, the existing limitations in section 5 of the act with respect to allowable deductions from taxable income of those whose income is derived from salary or wages be changed to provide for the deduction by each such taxpayer of the following:
(a)	Expenses necessarily incurred by him for board and lodging by reason of his employment at i distance from the place where he maintains a self contained domestic establishment.
(b)	Expenses incurred by him for transportation between his ordinary place of residence and his place of employment where, by reason of distance, he is required to live away from home to perform the duties of his employment.
(c)	Expenses incurred by him for depreciation and replacement of tools and special equipment or clothing which are necessarily required by him in the performance of the duties of his employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before putting the motion I hope Your Honour will consider whether or not it is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps I should read the proposed amendment to the committee. Mr. Barnett moves:
That the resolution be amended by adding thereto after item 23 the following:
24. That for the 1962 and subsequent taxation years, the existing limitations in section 5 of the act with respect to allowable deductions from taxable income of those whose income is derived from salary or wages be changed to provide for the deduction by each such taxpayer of the following :
(a)	Expenses necessarily incurred by him for board and lodging by reason of his employment at a distance from the place where he maintains a self-contained domestic establishment.
(b)	Expenses incurred by him for transportation between his ordinary place of residence and his place of employment where, by reason of distance, he is required to live away from home to perform the duties of his employment.

<c) Expenses incurred by him for depreciation and replacement of tools and special equipment or clothing which are necessarily required by him in the performance of the duties of his employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I think the hon. member pointed out, the brief submitted to me on this subject was dated July 8.
I have not had a chance to study it. It came in after the budget was presented. I would be only too pleased to consider it carefully before the next budget, but I would respectfully suggest that this particular motion is out of order at this stage because it would upset the balance of ways and means.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: After considering this motion it seems to me it should not be too difficult for the Chair to render a decision in connection with the proposed amendment. It is quite obvious that it is imposing a charge on the treasury, and it is a well known principle that only the crown can initiate a financial proposal such as this. I think, therefore, that the amendment cannot be proposed to the committee. Moreover, it is introducing an entirely new proposition; therefore it is irrelevant.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot say that your ruling has taken me altogether by surprise in view of the experience I have had. However I would suggest, as I did last year to the then minister of finance, that the minister on his own initiative should do something about this matter. I would be pleased to assist him by providing him with a copy of the draft amendment to the clause of the bill. I think this might cut down the amount of time necessary for his consideration. I have here-and I would be glad to send it across to him-a suggested draft amendment to clause 5 (2) of the bill for his consideration, in the hope that before we get to the committee stage he will have had an opportunity to take a good look at it and perhaps agree that it would be appropriate that it should be brought in with his consent. I will be quite happy to give the present Minister of Finance full credit if he will be the minister who finally completes the consideration begun by his predecessor, Hon. Walter Harris.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Would the hon. member allow me to ask him a question. In connection with this information which he has been kind enough to send me, I wonder whether he could give me some estimate of the cost in terms of government revenue which an amendment of this kind would represent. As he may remember, I am little concerned about a number of things in the economy, but one which has some bearing on this situation is the extent of government revenue and ex-
Income Tax Act
penditure. I should like to know whether he has any estimate of the effect of this on government revenue.

I cannot say that I have any estimate I would consider accurate enough to suggest to the committee. I am sure the minister has much better facilities than I to arrive at such a figure; but I am convinced, particularly if one gets down to considering the kind of detail which would be included in the actual text of a clause-and my draft is based closely on existing subsection 2-that with the restrictions and safeguards in such wording the effect would be quite insignificant in comparison with some of the other things which the minister has been prepared to undertake.

Mr. Chairman, I am disappointed with the response which the minister has made to this point. Not that I expected him to take it up, but it does get a little tiresome for representatives of the people, as we all are here, to keep taking this particular issue to ministers of finance and officials of the Department of Finance. On one occasion a few years ago representatives from the logging industry of Ontario and Quebec sat for more than an hour in the office of the minister of finance, and we were told- I do not think this is confidential any more- by a senior official of the department that the present situation was not fair in equity. The reason it is not fair is that construction workers have the privilege of charging expenses incurred by living away from home as a deductible item, yet people doing exactly the same kind of work in the logging and the bush industry cannot take advantage of this privilege.
The reason the logging industry missed out when the Canadian Construction Association and the Canadian Labour Congress managed to convinced Mr. Fleming a few years ago that they deserved this particular advantage is something that I have never been able to get clearly in my head. But I know from conversations we have had with department officials and with Mr. Fleming that the Department of Finance was perfectly aware that inequity exists in this matter. Therefore for the minister to say to the hon. member, who has brought this question up several times, as have I and other hon. members, "How much is it likely to cost?", is surely not good enough.
Last year I understand the Canadian Medical Association sponsored a seminar which took place on board a boat on a trip to Hawaii. Wives were allowed to go along and everybody had a good time. The seminar, of course, enabled the worthy doctors to charge

Income Tax Act
the trip as an expense. I know we smile at these things, but they come up all the time. We have had some vitriolics from the minister already with regard to expense accounts, but what we have in Canada today is a situation where people in professional occupations band together in organizations and hold conventions, and you have the old expense account business. They are able to take advantage of the act in a way that the ordinary guy-the little fellow, in the Prime Minister's words-has no opportunity to do at all.
I should like to point out that if the minister accepts the sort of amendment offered by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni he will be doing something for the genuine little guy in this country. By no stretch of the imagination are people like the loggers on the west coast and the bush workers of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes the kind of people who, for example, are going to be able to have seminars on their way home from Hawaii.
I suggest to the minister that if he checks with his officials he will find that they were disturbed when this exemption was extended to the construction workers. This is my opinion and I may be wrong, but I think the minister will discover that to be the fact. I will not say that the minister masquerades about this; I think he genuinely feels that as minister he has to be fair to all the people in this country. But as long as the logging workers and the bush workers cannot take advantage of this exemption, although their situation is in every way on all fours with that of most construction workers, then we have a real injustice embedded in the Income Tax Act.
The workers in my part of northern Ontario bring cases to me every year which I usually take up with the Department of National Revenue, and these workers cannot see why, if they have to go 300 miles from the city of Port Arthur to work as bush workers at a site which is right next door to a hydro construction project which is being carried on for a considerable length of time, they cannot deduct the cost of their board and room when they are also keeping a home in Port Arthur.
Yet the construction workers across the road from them are entitled to this benefit under the act. I hope the minister will get around to examining this, not from the point of view of removing from construction workers the entitlement they now have but from the point of view of extending it to other workingmen. Because this is the kind of group which needs assistance.
There is another group of workers in Canada with whose position I am quite familiar; that is the railway workers. In the main they are taken care of under the act when

they find themselves on the go most of the time. So far as the woods industry is concerned, that is the basic industry in our country. All other arguments about farming or anything else to the contrary, that is the basic industry. The men who prime the whole thing are the guys who go into the woods, get the trees, load them and get them out to the landings. They are the people who in so many cases do not have the opportunity to live at home; they have to go away to some kind of temporary camp in some other part of the country. Although there may be a trend this way, it is not yet the case in Canada that loggers live at the place they work. I think it is about time these people received some justice under the Income Tax Act, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has said.

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to support the argument which has been put forward, coming from a part of the country which produces a great deal of lumber. I do not know whether the minister is aware of it, but the city of Prince George is the western white spruce capital of the world as far as we are concerned. The situation which has been disclosed certainly merits the attention of the minister, and again I am pleased to see the Minister of Forestry is with us. I do hope he will whisper in the ear of the Minister of Finance and give a little support to this case. I know the minister is well aware of the situation. So I rise to support the contention which has been made. I think the arguments have been well put, and I hope the hon. gentleman will give serious consideration to providing some measure of relief for these people.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, after listening to what the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) had to say about a trip made by some physicians on a ship bound for Hawaii, I would like to point out that, as far as I know, expenses incurred through the presence of ladies on board cannot be deducted for income tax purposes.
Besides, many workers can take such trips if they are members of a labour union or a group which enable them to hold seminars. And if they want to choose Hawaii as their destination, I do not think that the Department of National Revenue sees any objection to it.
In addition, I must say that Social Credit, in its election platform, had a plank advocating an income tax exemption for equipment that workers must own. I fail to see also why the minister should not grant an income tax exemption with regard to trans-

portation costs incurred by workers when they have to earn their living away from their own home. Contrary to what was suggested to me by an hon. member a moment ago, it is not a matter of taking an exemption away from those who enjoy it at the present time, but rather to extend it to workers who are entitled to it also as Canadian citizens and human beings.
(Text):

Previous speakers have been championing the cause of the lumber workers. I would ask the Minister of Finance to consider the position of the people working in the field of exploration. Their case is even more deserving than some of those which have been mentioned many times today. As a rule they live in much more difficult circumstances. The camps in which they stay are almost invariably slight and temporary in nature by comparison with logging camps. Their expenses are considerable and they often work under conditions of great hardship, molested by flies and subject to all the inconveniences of life far from the comforts of civilization. These people, too, usually have to retain a permanent establishment in some place or other, and I trust the minister will consider their case when he is giving attention to other workers who come within this general category.

I just want to add my voice to those of other hon. members who have spoken on this subject. I support the remarks which were made in connection with the situation in the forest industry. I can speak with some knowledge of the forest industry, because I cut my first log in 1907. I have talked a lot about logs and I have written a lot about logs. I am not an academic logger.
I also wish to support the remarks made with respect to the mining industry. There are many employees in this industry who should receive special consideration because of the extra expenses they must incur by reason of their occupation.
I also wish to make a plea on behalf of the smelter workers. I am glad to see the minister look in my direction as I mention the smelter workers. I never rise to speak in this chamber on a question such as this without having in mind the industry at Trail, and I think of those men tramping up the hill to the smelter each day. Many of them, owing to changing circumstances of life and the difficulty of securing a place to live, have to stay in some cases 30 miles from their place of employment, and I suggest that consideration be given to the recognition of these unusual travelling expenses occasioned by the circumstances in which many of these men live.
Income Tax Act
When one considers that a commercial traveller, travelling long distances to sell, on occasion, quite unnecessary commodities, or insurance agents travelling all over the country, are allowed to deduct the cost of travelling from their income as a legitimate expense, I think the minister might well be asked to give consideration to the situation of those groups of employees which have been mentioned by previous speakers, and more recently by the hon. member for Kootenay West.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I would not like to see this debate come to an end before having had an opportunity to say a few words, since the Saguenay area of which I represent a county has lots of pulp-wood. There are in fact several lumber companies operating mills and therefore a great number of cords of wood are cut there each year.
The lumber companies, for some time now, have changed their way of doing. The method of cutting wood has changed and the workers now must get rather expensive power saws which do not last very long. I feel that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) makes a very important point since the lumber companies are in fact the only ones to benefit from mechanization.
Workers probably work less hard physically but, on the other hand, the work periods in the bush are shorter and expenses higher. The lumber companies no longer build camps where they have their logging operations; the workers must therefore get there by truck and give the contractor what it costs to take them from the camp to the work site. In my opinion, the situation having changed, the Minister of Finance should really consider the advisability of extending those exemptions to the bush workers who are quite often far from home for rather long periods and who are unable, because of that recent change, to bring home as much money as they used to.
I understand that this would entail a loss of revenue for the department but I feel that the act works against the small wage earners while sources of revenue that could greatly help the Minister of Finance to balance his budget are disregarded.
I find it strange that, during this debate, there was hardly any talk about how it would have been advantageous for Canada if the Minister of Finance had imposed a tax on capital gains. I am aware that Canada is one of the few countries where capital gains are not taxed. Such a tax is levied in Europe and

Income Tax Act
in the United States but not here in Canada. It is claimed that to impose a tax on capital gains would drive American investments away from Canada.
Well, if the minister felt it was appropriate, in the earlier introduction of his budget, to levy a 30 per cent tax on the sale of Canadian securities to Americans, if the United States government is now levying a tax on American investments in Canada, I feel that it would be wise for Canada to consider levying a tax on capital gains. I realize that it would be difficult to apply and that it would cover an extensive field because capital gains can include gains on the sale of capital investments, of buildings of any kind.
In my opinion, this tax could be levied against gains which accrue from stock market transactions. That sector remains untouched at present. Yet, it is a domain where huge benefits are made at the expense of the small man. As things stand at present, in Canada, when we have to find new revenue sources for the government, I feel that the minister would have been much wiser if he had levied a tax on the benefits made on stock market transactions instead of establishing an 11 per cent tax on building materials.
Mr. Chairman, it is my opinion that this matter should be looked into.
I realize that this matter was discussed neither by representatives of the Conservative party nor by those of the Liberal party, because they seem committed to the protection of the interest of large investors, more particularly the funds handlers.

Mr. Chairman, representations have been made with regard to those workers who have to leave their homes to carry on their way of life. I should like to say something on behalf of the railway workers. In this day and age when so many changes and abandonment of

railway lines are taking place, many elderly railway workers have found themselves faced with the necessity of moving to another place of residence. To them this is not economically sound. They feel they would like to retain their homes where they have lived for so many years, but they have to move to some other area to carry on their work. Many of them have complained to me about the fact that, like members of parliament, they have to maintain two places of residence.

Mr. Chairman, I too should like to support the representations made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and others who have spoken more recently, but I rise at this moment to ask the Minister of Finance to take a look at still another subject when he reviews the whole matter of the Income Tax Act. I refer to the right that is accorded to trade unionists and others to deduct their dues for income tax purposes. As the minister knows, that right is spelled out in subsection 10 of section 11 of the Income Tax Act. It is accorded not only to members of trade unions as defined in the act, but also to members of various other kinds of associations to which people belong for the purpose of improving their conditions of employment.
However, subsection 12 of the same section limits to a certain extent the amount of the dues that can be deducted. There are three limitations set out in subsection 12. The first two have to do with superannuation funds, pension funds, annuities and so on, and one can readily understand those limitations. As a matter of fact, unions that have pension plan payments included in their dues usually get deductibility for the payments into those pension plans under legislation with regard to pension plans as such. But the third limitation reads as follows:
(c)	for any other purpose not directly related to the ordinary operating expenses of the association or trade union to which they were paid.
Under this limitation it has been provided somewhere, by regulation or administrative decision, that trade unionists are not permitted in most cases to deduct the full amount of the dues they pay to their unions. I should like the minister to take a serious look at that situation. I do not expect him

to have the answer at this moment, but perhaps this can be notice to him that when we get to his estimates I should like to have a discussion of this matter.
For example, there are unions that go in for the construction of buildings which are necessary as part of the work of the union, and the members are required to pay a portion of their dues for these building funds. There are also other purposes that arise. Strike benefits sometimes impose an extra charge on members of unions. It seems to me that in all cases these payments come under the definition of money that members are required to pay to promote the improvement of members' conditions of employment and of work, and I regret that it has been found appropriate to make the kind of deductions that are made under the provisions of subsection 12, paragraph (c).
The result is that among trade unionists the percentage of their dues that they are allowed to deduct varies. Some are permitted to deduct quite a large percentage of their dues and some a much smaller percentage. As I say, this is a situation that has existed for quite some time. As far as I can ascertain, there has been no change in the practice since this provision was first brought in by Mr. Abbott when he was minister of finance I think the present Minister of Finance is undoubtedly looking for places to improve this kind of legislation. I hope he will take a good look at this point, and that if he cannot do something about it in the bill to be brought in momentarily he will be prepared to discuss the matter when we reach his departmental estimates.

Mr. Chairman, since we are now discussing section 11, paragraph 10, of the resolution concerning the Income Tax Act and because my riding, instead of enjoying the benefit of having vast industrial empires, has for the most part low income workers, especially bush workers who, most of the time, have to leave for the United States
Income Tax Act
where they barely manage to earn a living and suffer from the devaluation of our Canadian dollar compared to the U.S. dollar, I have a few comments to make.
Those people who, like many others, wish to come back home for the week end to discharge some of their duties as fathers, must pay for their transportation. It was pointed out a while ago that travelling salesmen, insurance agents and persons employed in several other fields, such as salaried workers and employees paid on commission, benefit from income tax deductions.
On behalf of the bush workers in my riding and the surrounding area-those people who, for over 20 years, have been given to understand that means are being sought to have them benefit from unemployment insurance when they come back for six months in their country-I cannot let this opportunity go by without asking for the revision of the income tax form for the low salaried workers and particularly the lumberjacks. In the Social Credit program there is an article which provides for the deduction from gross income of the cost of machinery and equipment that lumberjacks must get to work in the woods.
We also feel it would be advisable to revise the Income Tax Act as regards the salary of garage employees. Most of those employees are required today to have $300, $400 or $500 worth of tools, which they often break while doing their work. So if, in the case of certain jobs, the cost of equipment can be deducted from gross income, I think the time has come to consider giving bush workers and garage employees the right to deduct from their gross income the cost of the machines or tools they use in their work. Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise one other matter for the attention of the committee, in case it might have been lost in the shuffle of the political events that have occurred in the not too distant past. On February 4 of this year I received a joint communication from four volunteer fire brigades in my district. I had to reply on February 6 that, because of circumstances beyond my control, I could not do anything for the time being about the suggestion they brought to my attention. I do not know whether the present Minister of Finance has had any representations along these lines, but I have had a communication on the same subject from the same source since he took office.
I think perhaps I can briefly set out the point best by putting on the record a resolution which was passed by the British Columbia fire chiefs association in respect of volunteer firemen. It reads as follows:
Whereas the Department of National Revenue has recognized that all volunteer firemen have expenses in connection with their services, and
Whereas many volunteer firemen are not reimbursed for such expenses while others are, and
Whereas only volunteer firemen receiving remuneration up to a maximum of $300 per annum are eligible to claim tax exemptions, and
Whereas this discriminatory section of the Income Tax Act is not in the best interests of the Canadian fire service,
Therefore be it resolved that the B.C. fire chiefs association request the Minister of Finance to take whatever steps are necessary to have the Income Tax Act amended to allow a basic tax exemption of $300 per annum for all volunteer firemen.
I think it is obvious from the text of this resolution, and from the source from which I received it, that this is a matter which is of concern principally to the smaller brigades across the country who feel that they have been left out of the expense allowance which, in fact, is given to the members of the larger forces. speechtext: Have we completed the discussion on paragraph 1?

No, Mr. Chairman. We had a long discussion on this item on Friday and I do not propose to take much of the time of the committee in going over the ground which we covered on that day. This section, as we pointed out on that occasion, deals

with the principle of incentives under certain circumstances and to businesses of certain classes. It also has combined with it the definition of a corporation which has a certain degree of Canadian ownership.
The minister, in the course of a long discussion and questioning which we had on Friday, stated that one of the principal purposes of the provision was the modernization of Canadian plants and Canadian equipment. He pointed out that with a highly competitive economy it was very necessary to have the most modern, efficient plants and equipment. I think that is something with which every member of the committee would be in full agreement. He stated also that the other aim of the resolution was to create employment and stressed again, as he did in his budget speech, the fact that unemployment was one of the main problems of the nation. He suggested to the committee that when this resolution was enacted it would go some considerable degree towards the relief of unemployment, or in other words that it would contribute to a greater degree of employment.
At this time I am not discussing the principle of incentives. There are differences of opinion as to how much incentives may accomplish, but I am taking the minister's statements on these two points, (a) the modernization of equipment and (b) employment, and I say to the minister that if we accept that, as I am sure we all do, then it certainly is not necessary to have coupled with this paragraph the definition of a degree of Canadian ownership. The reason is that every plant in the country engaged in production, whether it be owned by a Canadian or somebody else, should have the most efficient machinery and plant possible. In other words everybody who can be employed should be employed.
To use the illustration I gave the other day, the mere fact that one person is working for General Motors and another person is working for Ford, and one company has a degree of Canadian ownership and the other does not, is a factor which has no relation to either of the persons who have jobs.
If this resolution is going to accomplish what the minister said it would, then I would suggest it should be given the widest possible scope and should apply to all plants regardless of ownership, provided they are operating in a legitimate manner in Canada. That can be done very easily when it comes to the bill, by the minister simply amending the resolution before us by deleting the definition in this paragraph. We all know the minister has strong opinions in this field, but if he is determined to go ahead with the propagation of his belief at this time, I would suggest that he simply drop the rest of the
Income Tax Act
paragraph and carry it over to the one dealing with the withholding tax, where it properly belongs. I suggest it has no place whatever in this paragraph, in view of what the minister himself said was the purpose of this part of the resolution.
He could accomplish the same purpose if the paragraph stopped after the words-
-if the property has been acquired by a taxpayer in a taxation year for a manufacturing or processing business in Canada.
If this were done it would cover all Canadians and would be of great assistance to both efficiency of plant and employment. I hope that when the minister brings in the bill he will consider this; but I repeat that if he feels strongly about this matter, as I know he does, then this definition properly belongs with the withholding tax and not here. I cannot help feeling that some draftsman in a hurry stuck it on the wrong paragraph, and that is all I have to say.

The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings mentioned the possibility that the minister might consider segregating these two parts of paragraph 1. I would be heartily in accord with that suggestion, in that I think that if more employment is to be arrived at there must not be any differentiation between two companies of a comparable basis, as for example General Motors and Ford.
With regard to the suggestion that the definition clause apply to paragraphs 6, 7, 8 and 9, I agree that the minister should give further consideration to this so that when he brings in the bill there will not be this discrimination and penalty against those now owning United States subsidiaries in Canada.
Let us consider for a moment what might happen if a company, in order to meet the requirements of this provision, were to dispose of some of its Canadian holdings. What would happen to the funds? They would go to the United States if it were an American concern. They would automatically go out of the country, and this would create a further strain on our foreign exchange. Also, if a company were to dispose of part of its Canadian shares I think it would undoubtedly take whatever surpluses there were in the company to the United States before disposing of Canadian shares, and this again would be a drain upon our foreign exchange.
I suggest that the minister give further consideration to this suggestion so that he might amend this paragraph to a degree that it would not be a penalty against foreign controlled companies. The incentive should be to Canadian investors to invest in equities in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There have been very important discussions with the American authorities over the last week. They were very cordial discussions and, as I said before, the American officials have been more than cooperative. Is he suggesting that this subject was raised?

I am not suggesting it was raised at that time, but I would be very much surprised if it were not. I cannot imagine your sitting down with the financial officials of

the United States and talking about financial problems without talking about this phase of them.
But I am saying that when we do raise these problems we might very easily be faced with the fact that because of our action in incorporating this principle it is very difficult for us to object if a similar form of action should be taken by the United States or any other country. We have the problem of renegotiating treaties. I am not going into the details here, Mr. Chairman. In his answer the other day the minister said no action had been taken with respect to renegotiation of the treaty or abrogation of its sections. I think it would be easy enough for us to renegotiate the treaty between today and the date the penal effect would become effective. I wonder whether any consideration has been given to that matter.
I remember a time not too long ago when we in this country had a succession duty treaty with the United States. As hon. members know, parliament in its wisdom decided to change from the principle of succession duty to that of estate tax. It was a different form of taxation but the principle was exactly the same. But what happened? We had a treaty, as I said, in which the words "succession duty" were used. We had to renegotiate another treaty with the United States incorporating estate tax. There was no objection to it in the United States; it was a relatively simple amendment to make; but I happen to know that the life of the minister of national revenue of that time was made miserable for two or three months by people who had been having taxes imposed without the benefit of a treaty, because they just could not find time, despite their willingness to co-operate, to get it through on the floor of the United States senate. This is not easy to do, despite the level of friendly relations that may exist between our two countries, and despite whatever promises may have been given by the executive. I presume promises have been given to deal with this matter rapidly. However, Mr. Chairman, I am suggesting that there will be difficulty in getting the treaty through on the floor of the senate, no matter how co-operative they want to be. We know how long it takes sometimes to get legislation through this house.
I think it would have been much better to have had the renegotiation take place before the cut off date, if any, is reached. We have given notice of it anyway. I think this would be better, rather than putting the cart before the horse and committing ourselves to doing certain things by a certain date, and wondering afterwards whether we are going to be able to renegotiate the treaties in order to do them.

I will not spend any more time on this question now, Mr. Chairman; I think we have already spent sufficient time on it. We will see the legislation when it comes before us. I simply want to say that we on this side of the chamber do not approve of this principle; we think it is bad. I suggest that this matter should be given further consideration. I read a newspaper article the other day which said the minister has had this principle in mind for ten years. I refer to the principle of greater Canadianism, which is a good principle. But if he has had it in mind for ten years, a few more months will not be much of a delay and it might be better to wait, say six months, to savour the atmosphere, find out what the developments are going to be and arrange for renegotiation of the treaties. Then things will move much more smoothly and quickly for the improvement of the economy of our two countries than I fear will be the case if we go ahead on this basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Excise Tax Act resolution which is now before the committee sets forth a variety of proposals in 17 numbered paragraphs. Before considering these individually it might be helpful for me to make some comments on the resolution as a whole. The most important provisions are in paragraphs 1 and 7, which provide for the withdrawal of the present exemptions for certain building materials and construction machinery with the effect of imposing a manufacturers sales tax on these commodities. Provision is made for new exemptions and for the continuation of existing exemptions as follows:
In paragraph 2, for municipal sewerage and drainage systems; in paragraphs 3, 8 and 9, for certain materials and machinery for agricultural purposes; in paragraph 4, for schools, universities and similar educational institutions; in paragraph 5, for certain components of buildings manufactured off site in competition with components manufactured on the construction site and exempt from tax; in paragraph 10, for materials used in newspapers and periodicals; in paragraph 11, for feeds for fish. Paragraph 12 proposes the withdrawal of exemption from sales tax for materials entering into the equipment and repair of private yachts and other non-commercial ships. Paragraph 13 is introduced to provide a greater measure of equity for the manufacturers of candy bars by withdrawing exemptions for certain confectionery products which resemble candy bars. Paragraph 14 repeals the existing export duty on electricity. Paragraph 16 provides for the application of the sales tax to previously exempt commodities in three stages, 4 per cent until March 31, 1964; 8 per cent thereafter until December 31, 1964; and 11 per cent from the beginning of 1965. Paragraph 17 provides relief in respect of goods sold and delivered prior to December 31, 1964 under certain fixed price contracts or tenders involving pecuniary penalties which were in effect prior to the budget.
It was indicated in the budget speech that the withdrawal of exemptions from building materials and production machinery could not be expected to be a popular move. I do not think that was an exaggerated statement. Tax increases are never accepted easily, particularly by those directly affected, and this is understandable. Nevertheless it was and still is my considered judgment that these amendments will be less harmful to the economy than the alternatives of obtaining
Excise Tax Act
similar amounts of revenue from any other tax sources. In order to obtain the additional revenues expected from withdrawing the exemptions for building materials and production machinery it would have been necessary to increase other taxes by very substantial amounts. For example, the government might instead have recommended a 33J per cent increase in the rate of sales tax; that is, from the present 11 per cent to 14J per cent. But to do this would have enhanced the marginal inequities which now exist between commodities subject to the sales tax and those which are exempt; and of course any move of that kind would have borne particularly heavily on people in the lower income groups. The government could have recommended the addition of a 20 per cent surtax on personal income taxes. This substantial increase would have had to be applied even at the lowest levels of income and this would have undoubtedly involved very severe hardship. In the present circumstances the government would not be prepared to recommend a measure of that kind. The government could have proposed the addition of 9J points to the rate of corporation income tax, which would have had the effect of increasing the top rate-that is, the 50 per cent rate-by 23 per cent. The economic effect on corporate industry of a measure of this kind would have been very damaging and the effect on employment would have been worse. Criticisms have been made of the measures we have put forward, and I dare say there will be more of them during the course of the discussion in committee. I suggest that anyone who wishes to criticize responsibly should try to indicate as clearly as possible-and I must say this was done by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands-the alternative course which he believes should have been adopted.
In addition to the measures and reliefs set forth in the resolution, hon. members may find it useful to be reminded of others. Special measures were announced in the budget in connection with interest rates and other terms of lending applicable to N.H.A. mortgages. These are designed to relieve the purchasers of new houses financed in this way from most of the burden of the increased sales tax on construction materials, and certainly all of the burden at the 4 per cent or even the 8 per cent rate. Important continuing exemptions from sales tax have been left untouched, including those for hospitals and those for homes for the aged. In addition I should refer to the exemptions in respect of farm machinery, crushed stone, sand and gravel and a list of goods purchased by municipalities.

We have listened while the minister has told us why he is imposing this tax on building products and industrial machinery used by two of our largest employers in this country-the construction industry and the manufacturing industry. This is the type of argument the minister has been putting up ever since he presented his budget. He has been explaining to us which is the less harmful tax and which is the more harmful, and why one should be applied rather than the other. In other words, he seems to have the impression that no one understands what he is doing and that he is the only one who is right, that everyone else must be wrong in the attitude they take with respect to this tax.
I saw a cartoon in the Globe and Mail the other day which, I think, reflected the hon. gentleman's attitude very well. It shows the minister driving up the wrong way on a one way street. The car he is driving is all battered; his glasses are shattered. A police officer, evidently, is nearby and the minister is saying to him: "But officer, you just don't understand". This is the situation which has been created in Canada by the application of the sales tax, whether it is levied in one lump sum of 11 per cent as originally intended or whether it is applied in stages. However it is put into effect it is bound to have a most harmful result in these two areas which employ so many Canadians. Instead of those industries moving ahead they will be restricted in their forward movement, and in the employment they are capable of offering, as a consequence of the application of this tax.
But the government has placed this parliament in a most peculiar position, because we have before us a set of budget resolutions which has replaced the original set. We agreed to this being done. It was done on the basis of unanimous consent. But this has given rise to a very strange procedure, particularly in view of the fact that the resolutions which were first presented formed the very basis of a budget. With these resolutions which we now have before us, we virtually have a new budget. This situation was pointed out in the Globe and Mail of July 10. The phrase was used-and I quote-"The second budget of Finance Minister Walter Gordon". If that is so, one is tempted to

Excise Tax Act
ask: what happened to the first budget? Well, it has been removed by a process which is strongly reminiscent of sleight of hand. There are those who have been telling us that the Minister of Finance is a financial wizard. Well, when it comes to making budgets disappear with nothing up his sleeve, the phrase certainly applies. I might say he is more than a wizard-he is a magician.
What is the position now with regard to the budget? After all, it must not be forgotten that the budget presented on June 13 received a vote of confidence. I might add that the party I represent did not participate in according this vote of confidence. But following that vote, the government expressed lack of confidence in its own budget by withdrawing the budget as it had been presented. Never, I submit, has there been such a situation of confusion compounded. The government has shown a complete lack of confidence in its own budget. It has swept it under the rug, I submit. The natural consequence should have been the removal of the minister responsible for the production of the budget or the resignation of the government. But neither of these courses has been followed. I want to emphasize that the responsibility does not rest entirely upon the Minister of Finance. Full responsibility rests upon the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues. It is a fact that the budget was not presented to the House of Commons without the Prime Minister's consent, and his approval of what it contained.
But neither of the courses I have mentioned has been followed. The government is going on as though nothing had happened. What it is saying in effect is: Let us forget about budget No. 1 and let us deal with budget No. 2. So this is the situation, the incredible position in which the parliament of this country finds itself owing to the ineptitude and confusion displayed by the government, an ineptitude and confusion unprecedented in parliamentary history. This confusion and ineptitude has been shown in the short space of time of two months since parliament convened.
These are the same people who accused the former government of creating confusion and indecision. All one has to do is to sit in the house and ask questions of importance to the nation. What do you get in reply from a government that was elected as a government of decision? We are told that a decision has not yet been made, that the matter is still under consideration.
The budget presented to parliament on June 13 last aroused a storm of protest such as has never been experienced before in the country. It was more than protest: it was

revulsion. It swept across all party lines. It came from business groups and organized labour. It came from provincial governments, and that is still going on, I might say. It came from municipalities and the stock exchanges. It came from all those who believed that what was needed was a fiscal and monetary program which would contribute to the expansion of the economy and provide employment.
It came from a lot of Liberals too.

Responsible individuals, responsible and representative groups of people with no partisan axe to grind, all knew when the budget was presented that it would not accomplish the objective of providing employment. They all knew that the budget as presented was going to bring about the opposite effect. They all knew that it was a bad budget.
This agitation by all these people throughout the country, which was stirred up regardless of their political affiliation, penetrated finally to the inner councils of the government. When I say "inner councils of the government" I mean that rarefied stratum where only the planners and the economic manipulators are persona grata, that haven of the theorists and the collectivists.
