speechtext: On a point of order, I suggest that the hon. member for Ontario, who was at one time a minister, should know the rules of the house and that he should refer to a minister as the honourable minister and not as he or she or it.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, after that nonsensical intervention I think I may carry on. Upon being questioned in the House of Commons the Prime Minister agreed that he would also seek the advice of organized labour and the farmers. And why not? When

the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance present another budget why should they not ask the advice of these people? It has been proven they were not able to do it on their own, even though they had the advice of whiz kids and students from universities.
We have been told that this budget is directed toward creating employment and cutting down on unemployment. This is the government that prior to and during the election campaign promised the people of the country that they would create full employment. All they wanted was a chance, 60 days of decision, and they would bring about full employment in the country.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council
speechtext: "No one will suffer".

I must say that this budget has been created to create unemployment instead of employment. Regardless of how the 11 per cent sales tax is applied, whether it is applied in three stages or one as was originally intended, the budget still is not one designed to create employment but rather to create unemployment. The 11 per cent tax applies to the construction industry, one of the biggest employers in the country in that it provides work for some 600,000 Canadians. One would have thought that a government that had in mind the creation of employment would have given an incentive, a boost, to that industry so that it would have been able to employ more people. But they have not done so. They have laid a tax upon this industry in order to keep it from expanding.
The government talks about giving an incentive to secondary manufacturing industry in Canada, an industry that employs Canadians on a year-round basis, an industry that was given incentives by the former government to the extent that they were able to increase employment by at least 2 to 2J per cent each and every year. That industry is now taxed so that it cannot expand, so it cannot maintain the percentage of increase that the former government was able to provide. Here are the two largest employers in Canada taxed by this government in such a way that they will not be able to expand.
The Minister of Finance has made some retreats in one or two areas from his original budget but he has not retreated from the imposition of the sales tax. All he has done is to modify it. He is going to apply it in three stages. This sales tax affects the workingmen of the country, but there is no retreat by the minister. He and the government are determined to tax the working people of this country and not give them any relief.
This was supposed to be a 60 days of decision government. Ninety days have now gone by and all one has to do is to look at the 28902-5-161
Excise Tax Act
record and he will find that it is a government of 90 days of indecision and confusion, of one fiasco after another. They do not need any help to create these fiascos. I submit that because of their actions and because of their failure to introduce proper legislation to help the unemployment situation they will go down in history as the government of unemployment. This government is now engaged in the business of crippling the economy of the country. All I have to do is read to hon. members some of the things that have been said in respect of the imposition of the sales tax. In the Ottawa Journal of July 11 the following appeared:
L. G. McKimmie, president of the Canadian Lumbermen's Association, said Wednesday the government's revised application of the sales tax on building materials and production machinery will continue to work hardships on the lumber and allied industries. He added that many small operators would be forced out of business.
That means lay-offs of men who are now employed.
The remarks were included in a letter sent by Mr. McKimmie to finance minister Gordon.
Did he pay any attention to them? He did not. Somebody gave him the idea that if he would modify this proposal and put it into effect in three stages, then the heat would be off and representations would stop.
According to the Toronto Telegram of July 10, the Toronto metropolitan homebuilders association intend to keep after finance minister Walter Gordon until it gets the budget sales tax on building materials wiped out altogether. I submit to the minister that this is good advice and he should take this advice if he is interested in promoting employment in this country and not promoting unemployment.
I should like to quote from an editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune of July 9:
_Mr. Gordon has in effect brought in four budgets. The first he brought down on June 13. The second came in on June 19 when he rescinded the proposed 30 per cent takeover tax. The third was read for him on June 24 by revenue minister Garland. The fourth came on Monday evening.
It must be admitted that Mr. Gordon improves as he goes along.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that is good advice to the Minister of Finance and if he wants to improve further along this line he should retract this tax which is going to be such an imposition on the economy of this country. I should like to list some of the protests from some of the industries in this country. I want to read extracts from a publication entitled "Industry", which is published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I read this from the issue of July, 1963:

Excise Tax Act
The measure of manufacturing industry's disappointment with the new federal government's first budget is the measure of the high hopes with which it was awaited-
Alas for great expectations. The dynamic incentives which industry, rightly or wrongly believed it had good reason to anticipate are not so dynamic after all. True, there are a number of corporate inducements of one kind or another in the budget but, for the most part, they prove upon examination to be restrictive and narrow in their application and consequently of limited value.
They say, in effect, they will be paying the tax twice over. This is not just, it is not wise and it is certainly not expansionist. If the Minister of Finance does not want to take advice from others, he should listen to us because we are in direct communication with the people in our ridings and the industries in our ridings. We know what they think about it. Certainly, at least, the minister should take the advice of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, because they are most reasonable in their representations, as history has proven.
In so far as my own riding is concerned, for instance, Ajax Magnethermic Canada Limited, an industry which has located in Ajax, Ontario, sent a letter to the Minister of Finance protesting this tax. They have pointed out that this is a tax which will lose employment for Canadians, and it is a tax on their income. It is a tax that has permanently lessened the prospects of employment in the purchaser's plant. They followed this up with a telegram which I received the other day. It reads in part as follows:
Further to our recent discussions budget apparently requires payment of sales tax on engineering drawings purchased from our U.S. associates so that we can build equipment in Canada. This increases our cost unfairly in competition with foreign competitors selling into Canada and furthermore constitutes double taxation since the added cost is reflected in our price on which we must collect sales tax from the purchaser.
Then, the automotive parts manufacturers association of Canada is protesting this tax. They have made representations to the Minister of Finance. A. C. Coulter, of Coulter Manufacturing Company, Oshawa, sent the following telegram:
Effect of sales tax provision on production machinery and tools is to worsen competitive position vis-a-vis imports of auto parts.
Then, we see more protests coming as listed in the Globe and Mail of June 18, 1963. In that issue of the newspaper we find Mr. McConnell of Edmonton, president of the national house builders association, protesting the imposition of this tax.

Then, we have the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities protesting against the imposition of this tax on building materials purchased by municipalities. The very capable mayor and capable members of the Oshawa city council have endorsed a resolution, a copy of which has been passed on to me to bring to the attention of the government. They feel that the imposition of the 11 per cent sales tax will be a great detriment to that municipality as well as other municipalities across the land.
However, the government has adopted a new attitude, a new technique. They say to the people of this country, we will give you this with one hand and take away even more with the other hand. We have the example of the municipal loan fund which is now being held in abeyance. The government promised that they would lend money to the municipalities at a low rate of interest and, as a result, there may be a saving of 1 per cent. There is also a forgiveness clause in this measure, the details of which we are unaware at the moment. They give this to the municipality, and then they turn around and tax the municipalities on the materials the municipalities are going to use as a result of the granting of these loans. Will there be a saving? This is something into which the municipalities will have to look very closely because you have the government giving them something with one hand and taking it away with the other.
All of these measures in the budget, naturally, have an effect on the employment situation, which is the prime concern of all Canadians and should be the prime concern of this government as it was of the former government. As a result of the actions we took we were able, for almost 24 months to decrease unemployment in this country month by month as compared with each month of the previous year. We find that since this government has taken office we have had an increase in unemployment for two months

in succession now, as compared with the same months last year. We are hoping that this trend does not continue, that this government will come out of its lethargy and introduce legislation containing incentives to the economy of this country that will overcome the situation I have described.
As an example of the very definite action we took while we were in office, directed at alleviating the situation of our economy, I would cite housing. House construction was undertaken on a scale on which it had never been undertaken in the history of this country. There was the drive for exports and the increase in labour-management co-operation which we brought about in this country through the productivity council. This council, which has done so much in this field, has now been discarded by this government. Our incentives to industry resulted in an increase in employment of 2\ per cent every year. Then, there was the winter works program which provided jobs for 100,000 every winter. This government has adopted this program, but has curtailed its effectiveness by shortening the applicable period by six weeks. These six weeks are the most productive of this program, and yet the government has shortened it by six weeks. What will the result be? Will 130,000 Canadians be able to get jobs under the program this winter? I doubt it very much. They have curtailed this program, not to help unemployment but rather to worsen it.
With regard to technical schools we provided space for 138,000 Canadians to learn new trades and skills, and the present government has adopted this program and added nothing new. Some 4,000 unemployed were trained in Canada in 1957; but last year, because of our incentives to the provinces, 38,000 Canadians were trained.
The government has also taken over our sewage disposal program. Our subsidies to the shipbuilding industry helped create employment in it, and we gave aid to the provinces and helped tremendously in the social justice field. Then there were our wheat sales; but now the Minister of Trade and Commerce says he is not responsible in this area.
What has the government done since it came into office? The most outstanding things have been the appointment of the cabinet and the two trips made by the Prime Minister. The Minister of Labour brought in nine points, but seven dealt with existing programs inaugurated by the former government, and two were gimmicks, one being the $500 for houses built within certain winter months.

What will this mean? There will be a tremendous bureaucracy of inspectors going around checking each and every home, when it was started and completed, to see whether it was built under N.H.A. standards and to find a reason not to give the builder the $500. It is nothing but a gimmick. Here is a case where the government offers something with one hand and takes it away with the other. There is another gimmick in the nine points announced by the Minister of Labour, the $75 bonus to an employer who employs workers over 45 years of age during a certain period. Where are the new programs the government was going to bring into effect?

Secretary of State says the budget has been adopted, I must disagree with him. AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I had just begun my remarks respecting the excise tax resolutions when the committee rose at six o'clock. At that time I was discussing the point of diminishing returns with respect to the government's stated intention of attempting to balance the budget, or of bringing the budget closer into balance. I believe it is fair to say that the government in its dealings with Canadian citizens cannot approach these matters in exactly the same manner as a corporation. In other words, one cannot look at the books and say that there are millions of dollars worth of sales, and that if a tax of 11 per cent, or any other percentage, is applied one can then multiply the tax by the previous year's sales and expect a revenue on that basis. We also have to realize that in the public affairs of this country sometimes a situation could develop whereby government
[The Deputy Chairman.]
expenditure would be greater than the anticipated revenue because of some disruptions in the economy affecting employment, and so on.
In addition to that, Mr. Chairman, I think we should accept the argument that the Minister of Finance has made that we need to do something to lower the deficits which Canada has experienced in its national affairs over the last few years. I believe that if we look at the increase in the national debt, the debt service charges which have been building up so rapidly, we cannot help becoming alarmed at the situation, and certainly any move to balance the budget or to try to balance the budget is a step in the right direction in slowing down this acceleration. However, I should like to suggest to the minister that increasing taxes-in other words, trying to increase revenue-is only one way of attempting to bring the budget into balance. We should also be looking at ways of eliminating expenditure which is equally as important as the other side of the ledger.
Looking back over the last few years, Mr. Chairman, we have seen enormous increases in the contribution paid by the Canadian people to the national debt. We have seen this in absolute terms of dollars and cents, and we have also seen the percentage of the interest charge on the national debt increased. I think the now famous conversion loan of 1958 added more to the expenditure side of the national account than any other single action of any government in Canadian history outside of wartime. I believe it is fair to say that this particular action of the government not only added a great deal to the debt service charges of that year, but that its effects will be with us in some cases for 25 years to come. While Conservative members are trying to make a lot out of the public protests which arose because of some of these additional taxes which were proposed by the minister of finance, they should remember that they did in fact create a situation in Canada during the last five or six years where it was necessary for a minister of finance, no matter to which party he belonged, to increase the revenue to take care of this additional expenditure. We in this party do not believe that that action was necessary. We do not believe it achieved any beneficial purpose for the Canadian people, and if it did it has not been thoroughly and adequately explained to this date. Perhaps here was another case of the government taking what was called bold, imaginative action and having it backfire on them, and consequently on the taxpayers of the country.
We in this party have over the years advocated that there should be some other

source of funds available to the government so that this tremendous increase in the debt service charges of the national treasury will at least be slowed down a little. We have said time and again that the Bank of Canada could be used to provide some of this capital which the government requires to expand the social services of this country. There are hon. members of this house and Canadian citizens outside this house who I believe do not quite understand just what it is the Social Credit party have been proposing with regard to having this capital supplied to the government. On occasions, some people just ridiculed the proposals we made. On others, people honestly and sincerely recognized the problem but did not understand the suggestions we were making as to ways of meeting it.
I have before me a series of articles written for the Winnipeg Free Press. They were carried on the pages of that paper in October and November, 1961. I am sure the minister would agree that the editorial writers and other writers on the staff of the Winnipeg Free Press are certainly not pro-Social Credit in their views. In fact, if anything can be said about them it is, I think, that they have unfalteringly supported the Liberal party over the years, whether right or wrong. So if I read certain excerpts from these articles I do not think the minister will brand them as additional Social Credit propaganda which can be dismissed as ridiculous or without foundation in fact. I want to read some of these passages so that we may lay a foundation for the proposals we are trying to make -a foundation which will gain some credence among people outside the Social Credit party.
Experts who are skilled in such matters will find that the relationship between currency, monetary inflation and sales of government bonds is direct and easily established. All that is necessary is to compare the amounts of the inflation with the government's offering of bonds and a little later, with increases in the assets of the chartered banks.
First comes the inflation-baiting the hook, so to speak. Then comes the bond issue. The public buys little. But the next time the assets of the banks are reported they show a corresponding gain in the holding of government bonds.
Here is another excerpt:
There is a wealth of statistics on money supply going back to early days. The pitfall for the unwary is that the only set of statistics which is based on a comparable dollar is the work of the research experts of the Bank of Canada, and have never been published. This set is available at the Bank of Canada at Ottawa but cannot be referred to usefully in this article because readers cannot easily verify the figures.
Accurate statistics for the years prior to the creation of the Bank of Canada are conveniently available in Professor Knox's study published by the Rowell-Sirois royal commission in 1940. Later figures are available in the statistics of the Bank of Canada.

The present figures appearing in the Bank of Canada weekly, monthly and annual reports go back only to 1947. These are readily available at any good library. For present purposes the record can start in 1950. Generally speaking, the years 1950 to 1957 when the government changed were -except for 1950-good years. The growth in the money supply was the normal growth required by a growing population and a growing national output.
Then follows a list of the total money-supply for each year from 1950 to 1960. I do not intend to read this list now, because there is a summary at the end which I shall
quote.
It will be seen that the increase under the Liberal government, after 1950, was about $500 millions per year, except for 1955 which brought an upward spurt of $1 billion. This is a period of just over six years. Except for one year-1959-the increase in money supply under the Diefenbaker government has been very great. Indeed, there have been two great inflationary splurges. In 1958, the increase was $1,324 millions.
I just put this on record so that the public of Canada may know that there is an increase in the money supply every year in a normal, growing economy and that there are years in which such an increase is substantially above the $500 million which is the average rate of increase during that period of time.
In this series of articles, the writer sets out to explain the technique used by the Bank of Canada to expand the money supply. He says:
The best way to explain ... is to give an example. The bank is the agent of the government. The government in the present year-
The year referred to is 1961.
-is spending $980 millions more than it receives in revenue from taxation. The government must, therefore, raise money by selling bonds and thus be able to pay its bills.
The article goes on:
In the illustration given, the government needs $250 millions. It is afraid to take a chance on the open market and so increases the money supply.
The Bank of Canada puts in an order with financial houses to buy any given amount of government bonds-say $20 million worth. The bond houses go on the open market and buy these bonds. They present themselves to the Bank of Canada the next morning and say "Here are the bonds you ordered. You owe us $20 million".
The Bank of Canada accepts the bonds and pays for them with a cheque-a small piece of paper worth, perhaps, 2 cents. The investment houses can do only one thing with that cheque-deposit it in a chartered bank. And the chartered banks can do but one thing with the Bank of Canada cheque. They present themselves before the teller's wicket in the Bank of Canada and deposit it in their account. The chartered banks are to the Bank of Canada what the mass of the people are to the chartered banks-customers.
I continue to quote.
Under the Bank Act. the chartered banks are required to hold cash or Bank of Canada deposits

Excise Tax Act
equal to 8 per cent of their own deposits from the public. This means that once the $20 million is deposited with the Bank of Canada the chartered banks can expand their own deposits by 12J times this amount-or by $250 millions.
The money supply is thus expanded by $250 millions by the stroke of a pen.
The chartered banks suddenly find themselves in possession of $250 millions of money or credit which they can lend. But they already had met all the credit-worthy demands. They had not been short of money.
So it follows, the banks use the $250 millions of new money to buy the $250 million bond issue which the government promptly issues. The government's accounts with the banks go up by this amount.
What has happened is that the chartered banks have increased their deposits by $250 millions and the money is thus dispersed all over the country-to contractors, manufacturers, civil servants, old age pensioners, and so on.
That is the end of the article. The point I wish to make is this: If this is correct-and we believe this is the way in which the increase in the money supply takes place- then why in the name of common sense cannot the Minister of Finance and the federal treasury go directly to the Bank of Canada, which is a publicly owned institution, and get the money there in the first place? If this were done, then the interest paid on this increase in the money supply would accrue to the Bank of Canada, which must turn its profits over to the treasury annually. I do not understand why we cannot use this means of increasing the money supply rather than having the chartered banks create an increase and then obliging the government of Canada to pay interest to them on something they did not have before this transaction took place.
Possibly there is a good, solid reason why this cannot be done, in which case I should like the Minister of Finance to explain to us. I bring this matter up at this time because we are interested in the minister's argument that something ought to be done to balance the budget-that something ought to be done to halt, to roll back, this tremendous increase in the debt service charge which is piling up year after year.
I think it is interesting to point out at this time that the increase in debt service charges for all of the years since 1958 is nearly equal to the deficits that have been incurred for those years. Even if this is so, if we had done something basic along the lines of what I am suggesting now so that the increase in the money supply would be made available to the government rather than coming to them as a debt, we would not be faced with nearly $900 million in interest charges this year and the deficit that the minister is forecasting simply would not have been necessary.

I wanted to bring this out, Mr. Chairman. It is not Social Credit propaganda. It was written by a man who has supported the Liberal party all through the years. We cannot undo or change something that took place years ago but we think that this can be done now. We are faced with this problem. We have got to meet the commitments that previous governments have made to the bondholders, but even a trip of a thousand miles begins with the first step and we can start now to do the financing of the federal government through this kind of action.
Just like Aberhart.

There are some gentlemen to my right who are using the same old kind of ridicule that we have been experiencing for the last 28 years. If it is ridiculous, I wish they would come forward with some kind of solution for the tremendous increase in the debt that has been accumulating, and the interest charges on it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the member for Medicine Hat a question. Is he against increasing old age pensions or baby bonuses? You cannot have your cake and eat it. If you are going to have these social services you have got to pay for them. If you are against any increase in social services, let us hear it tonight.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I hope you will take into consideration the loss of time they have caused me. The point I was about to make was that if the government would adopt some of the proposals we have suggested with respect to finding social capital or social credit

call it whatever you like-for the municipal development fund, that proposal would be one of the most far reaching and beneficial introduction by any government in a long time. I am not going to get into a discussion of that matter, because it will be coming up later; but the fact is that when the money supply is increased we believe it could be done directly by the Bank of Canada, and thus we would not have to sink deeper into the mire of debt where we are committed to pay increasingly large debt service charges.
In his opening remarks the minister asked for some alternatives and I suggest that he consider this proposal very seriously as an alternative, as a means of bringing the budget closer into balance. That is why I respectfully submit this to him.
There are one or two other matters I want to discuss with respect to the excise tax resolutions. One of them has to do with the administrative problems that the minister encountered respecting what is now referred to as the 30 per cent takeover tax. I realize it was withdrawn, but I bring it up now because the President of the United States has apparently proposed to congress a tax that is going to involve almost the same kind of administrative problems. As I see it, the major difference is that the tax will be 15 per cent rather than 30 per cent on sales of stock that would in effect transfer ownership of Canadian companies to Americans.
The other major difference is that the United States government and the United States treasury will be collecting the revenue, rather than the Canadian government under a proposal which, if enacted, will encounter the same kind of problem. If the President of the United States and his advisers have worked out some method of execution, if one may call it that, to overcome these administrative problems, I think it would be

Excise Tax Act
well for the Minister of Finance to find out what it is, because if the Canadian economy is going to have to deal with measures to restrict foreign ownership and foreign investment it seems to me it would be beneficial to the Canadian government and treasury if they could collect the revenue, rather than the United States government, because the effect is going to be the same. They are measures designed to inhibit the flow of capital from the United States and expand the ownership of Canadian industrial establishments in Canada. I realize, of course, that President Kennedy's proposals are much expanded over what the Minister of Finance brought in because they include bonds and securities as well as equity issues. In so far as this new plan will apply to equity stock, I think we should have some explanation of how the United States government plans to administer the collection of this tax and still avoid the administrative difficulties that caused the minister to withdraw his proposal. It would be interesting to know how this is done.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I think we have to realize that there is no balance between the $500 bonus that the department intends to extend to new homebuilders and the imposition of the excise tax on the building material that will be going into these homes. As the hon. member for Ontario pointed out, there will likely be at least $500 additional cost of construction simply because construction will take place during the winter as opposed to being undertaken during the summer. If one accepts that, and I think it is a reasonable deduction, then you are right back where you started. However, the addition of the 4 per cent tax on the cost of the material going into that home is going to be hung on to the mortgage, so the home owner will eventually have to pay, that is by the time the mortgage is paid off, at least $500, $1,000 or several times that amount.
In closing, may I say that I think we have to accept the argument that something ought to be done about this tremendous increase in the debt, and debt service charges. I urge the minister to give some attention to the administrative problem that will be encountered in connection with any particular measure before he introduces this in the house, because once a measure of this nature is introduced there are repercussions in the economy and in the stock market that are not easy to overcome. The other thing I should mention is that there have been some windfalls to wholesalers, and in some cases I do not believe the tax will be refunded to the customer.
This is not quite fair. I think the problem of imposing this 30 per cent takeover tax should certainly have been given far more consideration before it was introduced, in spite of the "60 days of decision". There were some rather heavy losses and some substantial gains as a result of the few days it was talked about in the house. The government did not increase its revenues as a result, but there were some people hurt while other people made fortunes to which they were not really entitled.

Mr. Chairman, the particular section of the Excise Tax Act now before us, of course, deals with the removal of the exemption of building materials, and it is to this I should like to address myself. This matter has been so widely discussed in the house and in the press that it is difficult to say very much about it now without endlessly repeating the arguments that have been made before. I, therefore, do not intend to take very much time of the committee. I will merely summarize our unalterable opposition to this tax and state that we will not vote for it when the resolution is called. Indeed, I hope to move an amendment at the conclusion of my remarks to emphasize our opposition to this tax.
We do not want to repeat arguments that were used in the budget speech, although since that time there have been certain changes in the budget resolutions. Some people have referred to this as almost a baby budget. Presumably, the baby is needed to take care of the miscarriage that happened to its predecessor. I listened to the remarks of the minister this afternoon with a great deal of attention, hoping that we would hear from him some clear, precise, intelligent and cogent arguments that would convince us to support this particular measure. As I understand the minister's position, his argument in favour of the tax is twofold.
First, there was his basic argument that we must somehow begin to move towards a balanced budget and cut down the national deficit and, second, that in order to do this we must find new sources of revenue. The tax that is being imposed in this resolution is the least unpleasant one that the minister could think of under the circumstances. Mr. Chairman, with both of those propositions we are in complete disagreement. We do not accept the premise that what is needed at the moment is a balanced budget. When you have a condition of chronic unemployment and regional underdevelopment such as we have discussed in this house, this myth of a balanced budget is a form of economic lunacy. What is really

needed at the present time or in the near future in Canada is a large, healthy deficit. We feel that a great infusion of capital should be made available; social capital is what we have called it. We have been asking for this since the commencement of the session, for large doses of social capital to be injected into the Canadian economy.
The member for Medicine Hat, who spoke before me devoted a great deal of his speech to outlining his party's fears of large national deficits. Other hon. members have done the same. I would only point out to the hon. member that this fear is not shared by many of the progressive governments of Europe. They have consistently run deficits for 10 or 12 years and, at the same time, have managed practically to wipe out unemployment and to have these social security benefits. The only thing about a deficit is that the percentage of your gross national product required to service it should remain practically constant. So long as this is done, large deficits present no problem, either in their financing or in their strain upon the economy of the country.
We do not accept the proposition of the minister, that what is required today is a balanced budget. We think this is a myth, economically unwise and unjustifiable. We also disagree with the particular form of taxation imposed here. This is a sales tax. As we said during the budget discussion, the sales tax is the most regressive form of taxation possible because it affects everybody in the community in a similar way regardless of the size of his income. We feel it is an unfair form of taxation. It is particularly unjustifiable in the case of a national government. Our provincial governments have to impose sales taxes, and have been forced into doing so because of their restricted revenue raising base. However, in so far as a national government is concerned, with all of the tax raising methods at its disposal, it is completely unjustifiable for that government to introduce a sales tax at this time.
For some strange reason the government has seen fit to single out for this new regressive tax one of the most sensitive sectors of the Canadian economy, and by that I mean the building and construction industry, and the manufacture of machinery for industry. It seems to us that by singling out this very sensitive section of the economy the government is setting in process of movement changes that will increase unemployment, decrease employment and cut the over-all revenue. We feel that to have singled out this particular industry is extremely unwise.
This action is 100 per cent incompatible with the government's expressed goal of full employment, because it holds out to us the hope of increased revenues while at the same 28902-5-1625

time it is setting in force movements and trends in the economy which will result in less employment and eventually less income to the government. It is a self-defeating piece of economic lunacy, shortsighted, incredible, discriminatory and just plain illogical.

I hope the minister will give us some evidence to indicate that this is truly a compensating factor; but previous speakers

have pointed out that this one quarter of 1 per cent reduction is more than offset by the increase in the cost of a home caused by this sales tax, and the increase in construction costs during wintertime.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I submit that it would be interesting, as it has been up to now, to hear the observations of the Minister of Finance. However, I submit also that this is not a good reason for abrogating the rules and practices that have been established in the house over many years. I am sure that most hon. members who were in the house during the session of the last parliament will recall a similar discussion on a similar point of order. But if I may go back to 1948, a similar point of order was then raised and determined by a vote of the house; that a resolution presented-
What page of Hansard?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
-by the Minister of Finance by way of a resolution that was segregated into paragraphs by numbers was in effect the same as any other resolution presented by a minister and no portion of that resolution could be dealt with paragraph by paragraph in committee of the whole.
In the 1951 Debates of the House of Commons, volume III, it will be seen that the then minister of finance protested a ruling of the Chair. A vote was taken in committee of the whole and the minister appealed the ruling of the Chair that a vote may be taken paragraph by paragraph. At page 2662 of Hansard of that session hon. members will see that a vote was taken and the decision of the Chair was reversed. There are a number of such rulings which have substantiated this premise, and as recently as the last session of parliament a matter of a similar nature was discussed. The hon. member for Winnipeg South, speaking to the question that was before the committee-that is, on the point of order that was before the committee as to whether the resolution should be dealt with paragraph by paragraph-had this to say. It will be recalled, of course, that the hon. member for Winnipeg South was on the opposite side of the house at that time. He sought to prevent a vote being taken on the resolution paragraph by paragraph, and pointed out substantially what I said earlier, that the excise tax and income tax resolutions are segregated for clarification and for no other purpose. I will read from Hansard of November 9, 1962, page 1477:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would just like to add one point to the very learned discussion we have had, contributed to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I wonder whether he has considered this fact. Although he was quoting from Bourinot with regard to a motion which might be divided into two or more distinct propositions. we are here dealing with a resolution, and a resolution is brought into the house and is followed by a bill. If the hon. member will look at the order paper he will find several resolutions there which contain several propositions; but the resolutions are written as a paragraph, divided by semicolons. It appears to me from a consideration of this matter that the budget resolutions are, for the convenience of the house, divided and numbered, rather than written all in one distinct paragraph with just the separation of a semicolon. Rather than being a whole series of distinct propositions, it is a resolution, just as other resolutions are, on which subsequently a bill will be founded and in which distinct measures are brought forward. That is perhaps a portion of the argument that was overlooked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he was speaking on this matter.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this argument applies equally to this proposition, and that this amendment is strictly and completely out of order having regard to the rules of the house.
Excise Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I do not claim to be an expert on all the citations that could be referred to with respect to the point of order that has been raised. When we look at citation 263 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, in paragraph 2 we find these words:
The principle that the sanction of the crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue.
Citation 265 quoted by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka seems to not altogether contradict that, except as regards the status of paragraph 1 of the excise tax proposals that are before us. It says, of course, that no member other than a minister of the crown may introduce a bill for the reduction of duties. However, further down it says:
This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed-
I do not believe that in so far as the committee is concerned the provisions contained in paragraph 1 have actually come into law, according to the stage we are at in this committee. In other words, the Minister of Finance is asking for the repeal of certain exemptions that were previously in effect; therefore they must be classified as "proposed" taxes, and if we are to accept the last sentence of citation 265 it would appear to me that the amendment moved is in order.
Hear, hear for the Social Credit.

Mr. Chairman, I, too, would like to speak on the point of order. May I first point out the very great importance of this point of order as indicated by the citation in Beauchesne already referred to by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. The point he makes in this regard is supported in the following phraseology, which indicates the importance of the matter before Your Honour.
What page is that?

It is page 221 of Beauchesne, citation 265, which reads as follows:
But the house enjoys complete freedom to make every representation possible to the government with regard to the manner in which the ministers discharge this responsibility.
Upon this ruling depends the exercise of what is described as the complete freedom of the house, which surely should be interfered with only in the clearest of instances. The citation then goes on with a surprising and delightful clarity which, Mr. Chairman, must make your task an easy one. It says:
This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration.

Excise Tax Act
That, Mr. Chairman, is precisely what the motion of the hon. member for Danforth does. The resolution proposes what is in effect a new tax. It is perfectly true that it takes the form of calling for the removal of a previous exemption from taxation, but the excise tax which is proposed is clearly an imposition of tax. Ask the building industry and the construction industry of Canada if this is not the imposition of a new tax. It being thus, the freedom of this house to perform its duty by proposing amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration is clearly indicated by this passage in citation 265. The prohibition referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay East- for a moment I almost mixed him up with the hon. member for Kootenay West, which would have been a horrible mistake-related, as I see it, to the sole responsibility of the government in levying taxes. We could move no amendment as private members which would levy a new tax, but in my submission it is perfectly clear from this citation that this historic freedom of the house is involved in this ruling which you are now called upon to make, but in which you are, as I said, relieved from anxiety in the matter by the clearcut terms of this citation.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps my perplexities as a new member may only add to the confusion but I would refer to Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 222, citation 268(1), which reads:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, example of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals. Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee, but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as an alternative duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown.
If this were not so it would destroy the means of recognizing the responsibility of the government in financial matters.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add my remarks to those made by my hon. friend the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour. Hon. members opposite have referred to citation 265 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. It is quite apparent from reading citation 265 that that is making reference only to bills and not to resolutions in committee of ways and means. Throughout it is clear that it refers to the power of the house in dealing with a bill, and we are
[Mr. Brewin.l
a committee of ways and means, a committee of the whole house dealing with a resolution. Beauchesne is quite clear on this point, where in paragraph (4) of citation 266 he says:
It is not in order to move the deletion of a particular clause in an excise tax resolution because it alters the balance of ways and means.
That is a very clear statement of what this committee can do and clearly shows that the amendment before us is obviously out of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Greenwood said that it would be a very grave error to get me mixed up with the hon. member for Kootenay West. I can assure him that I would feel very badly about that, but the mistake would be in his favour. I want to point out, in support of the argument of my hon. friend from Vancouver-Burrard, that the point of order is not that we will be so much impeding the balance of ways and means, but rather that this is a resolution not a bill and cannot be voted upon clause by clause. It can be agreed that discussion cease on various clauses, but there can be no determination by a division of the house on the resolution stage. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that you have no alternative but to rule this amendment out of order.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I marvel at the number of members on the government side who think this matter is clear and straightforward. I suggest that the hon. member for Kootenay East has come close to the heart of the point, but he has come at it from the wrong side.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am not a left winger; I am a right winger.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I hope that remark is on the record. To get back to the point of order, hon. members realize that if the objection to this amendment is sustained we are put in the position which the hon. member for Kootenay East said we should be put in, namely that we have no right to express ourselves as a house on paragraph 1 of the Excise Tax Act resolution. In my view we are still suffering from the mistake which was made in 1948 when the house, by a vote, reversed a ruling which had been made by the chairman of the committee of ways and means at that time. Up to that time we had followed the simple, logical, understandable course of voting on the separate paragraphs of a budget resolution as they came along.
What is before us now is paragraph 1 of the Excise Tax Act resolution. It is a proposition complete in itself. Yet the hon. member for Kootenay East says that somehow the rules must be interpreted in such a way as to prohibit us from having the chance to

vote on this section of the resolution. Because we are caught with that ruling of 1948-actually it was not a ruling, but a vote by the majority of the house against the ruling of the Liberal member who was in the chair at that time-because we are stuck with that, we have no other way to get a decision on individual paragraphs than by moving, as the hon. member for Danforth has done, that a particular paragraph be deleted.
I submit that after all the citations have been read on both sides the simple, common sense, logical position is that the House of Commons of Canada ought to have the right to vote on this proposition by itself. I submit that the most recent precedent occurred in this very committee only yesterday. Yesterday, my hon. friend from Winnipeg North moved by way of an amendment that paragraph 4 be deleted from the income tax resolution. The hon. member for Kootenay East was not on his feet then telling us we could not do it, and all these other people were not raising points of order. Of course, there were only a dozen or so of us who were prepared to vote for that amendment; but I submit that since the Chair yesterday allowed the hon. member for Winnipeg North to move the deletion of a paragraph from the income tax resolution a similar view should be taken today with respect to the excise tax resolution.
In both cases an attempt is being made to do a simple, common sense thing, namely to vote on the proposition which is before us. The minister has placed his thoughts before us on paragraph 1, and if we are no longer permitted to vote on these resolutions paragraph by paragraph, then I submit we should follow the precedent set yesterday when an hon. member moved to delete the paragraph.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I wonder if we have not heard sufficient argument on this point. As to the proposed amendment, I must say the Chair is ready to make a ruling and that additional argument would not be helpful in any way.
I should like to refer first of all to the point just made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who referred to the fact that yesterday the committee was allowed to vote on a similar amendment. The Chair was well aware of the difficulties which might arise from the standpoint of correct procedure in connection with that particular amendment; but as everyone knows, who was in the chamber at the time, no point of order was raised in connection with it and I felt I should not intervene by bringing up the question. That is why I allowed the committee to divide on the substance of the amendment. However, I do not think a precedent was set. As I say, I was fully aware
Excise Tax Act
of the implications of what was done yesterday. I had before me then the decision reported in Hansard, of November 9, 1962, and I felt then, as I feel now, that no precedent was set.
To come to the particular point involved: paragraph 1 of the resolution before us proposes a tax. The amendment, to my mind, has an exactly opposite effect. Indeed, it destroys the proposal we have before us. It is not properly speaking, an amendment. It is a negative. In other words, it is an entirely new question which is now proposed and it would appear to me, if only for this reason, that this is sufficient ground for reaching a decision that this is not a proper amendment.
A moment ago the hon. member for Kootenay East brought up the point to which I referred, with regard to the decision of the house made last year. This decision can be found in Hansard of November 9, 1962 and I should like to read in part the ruling which was then made by Mr. Chairman Chown who said at page 1477:
While I rose, perhaps instinctively, on the suggestion there should be a division on the section. I realize that I moved in haste and overlooked the authorities in support of the point of view I am now making, namely, that there should not be paragraph by paragraph division.
My authority for that, briefly, is May's sixteenth edition, pages 411 and 412. Perhaps 1 might read a very brief portion of this passage on page 412 which is helpful to us.
"The house does not recognize the right of individual members to insist on the division of motions moved in committee of the whole house or of motions giving special facilities for the transaction of public business-"
Of course, I am quoting only in part. I should like to refer directly to page 411 of May's sixteenth edition where we read:
In 1770 a motion "That it is the rule of this House, that a complicated question which prevents any member from giving his free assent or dissent to any part thereof ought, if required, to be divided," was negatived on a division. As late as 1883 it was generally held that an individual member had no right to insist upon the division of a complicated question.
For these reasons, the Chair cannot put this amendment before the committee.

With great respect, Mr. Chairman, I appeal your ruling to the house.
Mr. Deputy Speaker resumed the chair and made the following report:
The question is an appeal to the house as follows:
When a resolution to amend the Excise Tax Act was being considered in committee of ways and means, the hon. member for Danforth moved the following amendment:
"I move that the Excise Tax Act resolution be amended by the deletion of paragraph 1."
The Chair decided that the amendment was in effect a negative and was out of order as in accordance with recent practices and decisions of
