the house a vote could not be called on a particular section of a budget resolution. Whereupon the hon. member for Danforth appealed to the house from the decision of the Chair.
Mr. Speaker put the question as follows:
When the resolution to amend the Excise Tax Act was being considered in committee of ways and means, the hon. member for Danforth moved the following amendment:
"That the Excise Tax Act resolution be amended by the deletion of paragraph 1."
The Chair decided that the amendment was, in effect, a negative and was out of order as in accordance with recent practices and decisions of the house a vote could not be called upon a particular section of a budget resolution. Whereupon, the hon. member for Danforth appealed to the house from the decision of the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was paired. Had I voted, I would have voted to uphold the ruling of the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was paired. If I had voted, I would have voted to uphold the ruling of the Chair.
And the house having resumed in committee:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the resolution carry?
Mr. Chairman-
Oh, oh.

It is nice to know, Mr. Chairman, that the boys are in here earning their $10,000 tonight. I wish to bring up a particular matter relating to paragraph 1, although it specifically deals with paragraph 4 of the resolution. It is the question of what classification the institutions known as public libraries will receive under the general purposes of the first part of the resolution.
I suppose the minister is aware that the way the provision reads at present, any kind of university construction would be entitled to the exemption. Therefore a university library would be entitled to it. Libraries within colleges and universities will have the

exemption, but the public institutions supported by communities or municipalities, or even endowed, will not be able to take advantage of it.
The minister must be aware that a public library to all intents and purposes is accepted as an educational institution. It is certainly accepted as such by the teaching profession. I took the trouble to call the Department of National Revenue, but the official who is supposedly responsible for interpreting this part of the resolution gave me to understand that public libraries would not be exempt.
I also think the minister is familiar enough with the penury of public libraries. He has an example in his own city where Toronto public library recently had difficulties in getting funds, and he must know that this imposition will hurt the construction of public libraries much more than it will secondary and primary schools in some parts of the country. Indeed, in Toronto itself the board of education has more facilities in terms of finance and the capacity to raise capital than the public library board.
For that reason the minister should give us some kind of declaration, right at the very beginning, as to what consideration he is going to give to classifying public libraries as educational institutions.
I know that if someone speaks about public libraries someone else is likely to bring up the question of art galleries and museums, but in effect throughout most of the country public libraries serve as museums and art galleries, and I think in general that part of the community which reads, studies and is interested in adult education would approve very heartily of public libraries being exempted.
I understand the minister has received representations on this point from the Canadian library association, and I can tell him that in my own constituency two communities intend to extend their library facilities within the very near future. From experience I know that the library boards in these communities have much more difficulty than boards of education in raising money. They will be especially hurt if public libraries are not included under the exemption set out in paragraph 4 of the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder if I might reply to this question now?

I just have a few remarks to make on the same point. I was going to leave them until we had reached paragraph 4 where universities and educational institutions are defined, but I want to support the plea made by the hon. member for Port Arthur. Generally speaking libraries are in
Excise Tax Act
the same classification as educational institutions. They do have unusual difficulties because in many cases they are not part of municipal councils or municipal set-ups, and in some cases they form a more or less volunteer organization. They perform a very good public service at a very low cost, and I would certainly support the proposal of the hon. member that libraries should be specifically included in the definition contained in paragraph 4.
Mr. Chairman, before the minister replies I wonder whether I may have about 45 seconds to ask him-
To clear yourself.

-this question. I was going to wait until clause 4 was under discussion to raise this question with respect to public libraries; however, there is one specific question I wanted to ask the minister. Is the government taking into consideration the limit on financing imposed by reason of a bylaw in a municipality which has been passed to provide the authority to borrow funds to build a library? I ask this question because the municipality and the local library board are confined to the limits imposed by the bylaw. Of course, if they classify them as educational institutions, that automatically takes care of the matter. On the other hand, if the minister does not intend to designate libraries as educational institutions, I wonder whether he would care to comment on what consideration the government will give to these bylaws which impose limits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think all hon. members will appreciate the fact that there is no complete equity in taxation, and as soon as you start to grant exceptions it is a question of where you draw the line. This particular problem of the libraries has been raised with me over the last several days by the hon. member for York-Humber, who is particularly concerned about a public library that is contemplated in the town of Mimico.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman laughs, but I am being quite serious. This is a point, and I have been giving it consideration. My difficulty is that if the line of exemption is moved, the question is where do you draw that line? Unfortunately, or fortunately, all public libraries are not operated in the same fashion. In some cases everything is free; in other cases only certain things are free. Then, of course, you get to the stage where it is operated on a semi-commercial basis. I can assure my hon. friend that the members on this side of the house are very

Excise Tax Act
interested in libraries and in books. I believe it has been mentioned that some of us have even had the temerity to write books. We do not think that is anything to be ashamed of. I think it is fair to say that quite a lot of us read books, as do many hon. members across the way. But this is a difficult point upon which to draw the line, and we have decided that the line cannot be extended.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is rising on a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I hesitate to raise this point of order against the hon. member for Waterloo North, but I think it should be drawn to the attention of the committee that it is against the rules of the house to quote from a document which reflects upon proceedings which are taking place at the time. If I may quote citation 149 of the rules of the house, there are a number of rules or prohibitions, and (1) says that a member must not:
-read from a printed document or book commenting on any speech made in parliament during the session;-
I might also refer to Beauchesne's third edition, page 802. According to that page Mr. A. E. Ross, the acting deputy speaker, ruled that it was out of order to quote in committee articles from newspapers commenting on the proceedings then under consideration. Objection was taken and a division followed, and of course the ruling was sustained. I suggest that if the hon. member were going to limit his quotations to one or two documents, that would be all right; but to make up almost his entire speech from quotations from people not participating in the debate is completely contrary to the rules.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point taken by the hon. member is a good one, to a degree, and I am sure that the hon. member will want to keep that in mind in the course of his remarks.

Excise Tax Act

Thank you, Mr. Chairman; and I hope the hon. member who was speaking will do the same when his turn comes.
In writing to the Minister of Finance on June 29, 1963, Hogg Fuel and Supply Limited of Waterloo voiced its objections in this way:
I would like to voice our opinion in as strong words as possible, our objections to this sales tax on building supplies and machinery. Not only ourselves but the whole industry is in a state of confusion. We can get no answers from anyone. Our serious belief is that you will kill industry and business. The cost and uncertainty of this tax is terrible. Our belief is that our business is going to suffer extremely through this tax, and therefore profits will drop and defeat the purpose of this tax.
Mr. Kay Bauer of Bauer's Limited, Waterloo, manufacturers of cotton felts, automobile pads, and so on, sent me a copy of a letter which was sent to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association at Toronto, in which he asked for clarification of the 1963 federal budget and the proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act. He also stated that his firm considered the repeal of the sales tax exemption on building materials, and especially on production machinery and processing materials, to be a very retrogressive step, to say the least. He said it would add considerably to the manufacturer's cost of production and be yet another handicap in his fight against imported goods. He also added that the government not only proposes to increase his costs drastically, but is also proposing to reduce our tariff protection under tariff item 559g from 20 per cent to 17 per cent, most favoured nation. Mr. Chairman, there is not much consideration for Canadian industry in this budget.
Mr. Vincent McHale of the Siegner Lumber Company of Kitchener, in a letter to the Minister of Finance, had this to say:
It is my contention that by placing this sales tax on building materials you are penalizing the person who wishes to buy a home, who under most circumstances is the most productive and the type of citizen Canada needs and wants.
Mr. Chairman, the lumber industry is one of the few, outside of mining, which contributes considerably more to the provincial and federal governments than it gets in return.
The automotive parts manufacturers association (Canada), of Toronto, of which many firms in Kitchener and Waterloo are a part, have written to me concerning this sales tax. They expressed their views in these words:
It is the belief of the automotive parts manufacturing industry that the present increase in taxes from zero to 11 per cent can only lead to increased prices which cannot be tolerated in this industry. The automotive parts manufacturers association of Canada has requested the hon. Minister of Finance to repeal the withdrawals of the exemptions.
[The Chairman.}
Another copy of a letter of interest sent to me, addressed to the Minister of Finance by Mr. Jean-Guy Maheu, executive vice president of the shoe manufacturers' association of Canada, which has a large number of firms located in my area, gave his impressions concerning this tax in these remarks:
Faced with intense competition and rising imports of foreign made footwear, our Canadian manufacturers have successfully held the price line for footwear in the past as industry profit margins have dwindled. The new sales tax, however, contributes substantially to our factory costs of operations, and footwear prices will soon reflect this new federal tax burden.
In addition, several companies report that they will defer or cancel orders for new machinery as a result of the new tax and this action will, in time, leave them with less than the best of equipment to compete with foreign footwear at this critical time.
Another important association which has protested this cost increase and which is well represented in Waterloo North is the Canadian Construction Association. They have urged that the proposed application of the federal sales tax to all construction materials be deleted from the budget resolution. These people play a big part in the economy of our country, and I hope the minister will give serious consideration to their request. Objections I have received from my riding include those from such well known firms as Canada Barrels and Kegs, Waterloo, the Sign Association of Canada, represented by A-K and Lippert Plastics in Kitchener, Sehl Engineering Limited, Kitchener, under the management of Mr. John Vingoe, and Campbell Machinery Limited, Kitchener. These firms have lost a number of orders already, and feel that the new sales tax will affect them considerably, both in buying and selling. Some even find they will come to a standstill.
I am sure the minister will realize that with such criticisms and objections coming from the many firms I have mentioned, and others too numerous to mention, it could well be that our unemployment situation will rise. We will be paying out huge sums of money through our unemployment insurance fund to these many unfortunate people without work, people who could, with the cancellation of this tax, be making a real contribution to the growth of our country and a happier life for themselves and their families.
An editorial in the Kitchener-Waterloo Record of July 11, said the measures introduced in this lamentable budget were obviously ill suited to the task of raising money. Their long range effects may even be highly detrimental to the general economy. Another paragraph with which I heartily agree said:
It has been remarked by more than one Canadian that an increase in the income levy would

be fairer and surer. There would have been protests hut it is almost certain they would have died away after a relatively brief time.
When the budget came out and, again, when changes in it were made there was criticism that fortunes had been won and lost in the fluctuations of the stock market.
There is a parallel situation here in respect of this 11 per cent sales tax, even when applied in stages. A lot of money is being made by building supply dealers with big inventories, just because the budget provisions concerning this tax were not clear when they were imposed. While some dealers have not raised their prices, others have, and the tax now applies to building supplies which might have been in their inventory for months. It is just like found money, Mr. Chairman. These dealers are lining their pockets with money which should be going to the government.
While the government has made these moves, which will definitely hinder building activity, it has done nothing in the way of allowing the refinancing of older homes-a move which would do more to help the housebuilding industry than any $500 bonus the government could devise.
Government spokesmen promised during the election campaign that the refinancing of older homes under the National Housing Act would be made possible. Why is not such a system in operation here? It has worked well for years in the United States. I suggest to the government that some consideration be given to a plan whereby older homes could be refinanced under National Housing Act regulations, though it might be wise to look into it more thoroughly than were some of the budget regulations before the legislation is enacted.
The Minister of Finance mentioned in his address of July 8, 1963, that the government proposes two changes of substance in the excise tax resolutions. The first of these concerns schools and universities and similar educational institutions. This is a step in the right direction and should assist my two universities in my riding of Waterloo North, the University of Waterloo and the Waterloo Lutheran University along with collegiates and other schools. The previous government did much to help universities, and I hope the present government will continue to make such assistance available.
My remarks have been of a constructive nature, Mr. Chairman, and have, I hope, brought to the attention of the government the sound thinking of thousands of Canadians concerning this unfair tax. I sincerely hope the government will reject this tax so that
Excise Tax Act
the people of our country may know, finally, where they stand economically in the coming year.

In speaking to this resolution, Mr. Chairman, I shall express my views on the matter and make some reference as to how my own area will be affected. Many observations have been made on the budget and on its preparation. One which was of particular interest was made by the Prime Minister recently when he said that the traditional methods of producing a Canadian budget were no longer adequate to the country's needs. The right hon. gentleman suggested that changes would be made in procedures so as to enable the government to consult with business before another budget is prepared. That is nothing more or less than a smokescreen.
This government did not make use of the information and knowledge which are readily available to them. The personnel of the finance department are in possession of a wealth of experience accumulated over a long period of years. Without a doubt, they are keen students of our economy and its requirements. Given the opportunity, they could have charted a safe course for the Minister of Finance and thereby averted the severe set-back in our economy, as well as the many unnecessary inconveniences caused by the current budget. The minister preferred to make a bold new approach by consulting amateurs who led him down the garden path to budget chaos.
On launching his budget, the Minister of Finance told us that someone had given him his horoscope for that day, which read, "Don't worry over money matters". The measures proposed in the budget would indicate that the minister had, indeed, been heeding such advice during the period of its preparation. He made many decisions on money matters which at the time did not worry him, but which have since given the Canadian people much worry, and himself a severe headache.
The three ghost writers must have absorbed a good part of the worry in connection with the budget during the course of its preparation. However, Mr. Speaker, it appears that they shared the mental lapses of the minister and between them they came up with a document that, had it not been for last minute adjustments, would have made a complete shambles of the economy which a Conservative government had well on the way to boom proportions.
Perhaps the most flagrant disregard for what the repercussions might be was the introduction of the 30 per cent takeover tax. This measure immediately created confusion and frustration on our stock markets and

Mr. Chairman, I thought for a little while this evening that the debate had proceeded to the point of a detailed consideration of some of the issues in the resolution, but I find that it has now turned back to a more or less general discussion of the principles involved. I am glad, because this gives me an opportunity to take part in the debate and outline in a general way our position relative to some of these matters.
I think it is doubtful that any proposal in the field of taxation has ever met with such a storm of protest as the one before us tonight, the withdrawal of the sales tax exemption on building materials and production machinery.
I agree with the Minister of Finance, of course, when he says that no tax is popular, but it seems to me this one is especially obnoxious in that it not only reduces still further the purchasing power in the hands of the people but also threatens the very objectives it proposes to realize. If I understood the statement made by the Minister of Finance correctly, he pointed out that one of the objectives was the balancing of the budget or at least bringing our financial affairs into closer proximity to a balanced budget. The second was the creation of employment opportunities. Another one was the expansion of the economy. I am sure that these various matters to which the minister has called attention are of vital importance and they have been dealt with by various speakers throughout the day.
I should like to refer, first of all, to the announced intention of endeavouring to balance the budget. I know that the hon. member for Danforth ridiculed this idea. He said it was not desirable, and it was something that should not be sought after. But I believe that the present picture as it relates to our national debt, and to the cost of servicing the national debt, would point up very definitely the importance of doing something in this field of endeavouring to balance our budget. I should like to refer to the statement made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. The hon. member made some suggestions and asked the minister if he would reply to those suggestions. Unfortunately, the Minister of Finance has not done that as yet. This reminds me of the fact that a number of years ago Social Credit members in the house made some suggestions relative to monetary and financial reform. A great deal of criticism was levelled against us, not only by members of the house but by some of the newspapers.

Excise Tax Act
A newspaper in eastern Canada, the Fundy Fisherman-I am sure many of us know who is the publisher of that paper-in an editorial said that it would take more than ridicule to get rid of Social Credit proposals in the field of monetary and financial reform. I recall another occasion when I was speaking in the house and I asked the then minister of finance if he would outline his views relative to the proposals we were advancing. We received the same silent treatment as my colleague from Medicine Hat has received today in relation to his request. I would suggest that before this debate is brought to a conclusion, the Minister of Finance should reply to my colleague and give some reason for his inability to accept these suggestions. He should outline the weaknesses in these proposals so that, at least, if they are not satisfactory we will know there is no use proposing them again. So long as we are met with silence in connection with our proposals, we are likely to keep pounding along making them time and time again until perhaps we do get some response from the Minister of Finance.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that since this measure has been outlined as one of the measures that is aimed at the objective of balancing our budget, then these things should be taken into consideration. I believe that the steps that have been taken will lead us to the point of diminishing returns. The minister pointed out a number of rises in the cost of material and indicated they had not caused any disruption so far as construction is concerned. In other words, he seemed to imply he was going to work on the principle of putting on as many taxes as the traffic will bear. I suggest if we take that attitude, if we continue with that principle, then we are going to reach the point where we stifle production, where we stifle construction and instead of increasing our revenues we will find our revenues decreasing.
In so far as employment opportunities are concerned, it would seem to me that the implementation of the proposals now before us would just work in reverse. I, as well as many other members in the house, have received many communications. I am not going to read them, I am not going to give them by name. I just refer to this matter and say we have received these communications indicating that project after project has been shelved or delayed and, in some cases, businesses have been closed up, productive enterprises have ceased to exist, men have been thrown out of employment.
Of course, when men are thrown out of employment they go on the unemployment insurance list and receive payments, thus putting a further strain on a fund that has been in serious difficulty in the past. It

would appear to me, Mr. Chairman, that the objections that have been raised, so far as this particular aspect of the resolution is concerned, are very sound, and instead of promoting employment opportunities they are going to throw men out of employment, cause further unemployment.
The third point was a reference to the expansion of the economy. I believe the periodical "Industry" published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association was referred to today. I should like to quote this very short paragraph from the periodical:
In short, the effect of this extension of the sales tax can only be to slow down economic activity, hold down employment, inhibit competitiveness, retard productivity improvement and generally act as a depressant rather than a stimulant.
Now, that seems to sum it up. The minister may take objection to some of those suggestions, but nevertheless I think they should be given consideration. I had a communication from Mr. Pybus of the industrial development commission of greater Vancouver with reference to this whole matter of expansion of the economy. Perhaps I should just make a brief reference or two to this particular letter. He says:
We in British Columbia, as across the prairies and in the maritimes, are fighting to expand and develop new secondary industries in order to create job opportunities for our young people and our growing work force and a better balanced economy. We cannot reconcile this setback for growth in job-creating industries with the Liberal party's espoused sympathy for and policies to expedite economic growth which gave much hope to the great numbers in need of work.
Now then, what are some of the categories that are affected by the removal of the sales tax exemption from this particular item? First of all, we think of the potential home owner. I recall many members in the house in other days speaking of the importance of our people owning their own homes, emphasizing the fact that every encouragement should be given to our people to own their own homes, because it gave them a sense of security and well being that nothing else could give. I am sure that today we all agree with the desirability of home ownership. We think of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, an institution which I believe is designed to make home ownership possible. On the other hand, when we look at the other side of the picture we find that the imposition of this tax is going to work in the opposite direction. It has been pointed out that a $500 bonus has been offered to people who build in the wintertime. Well, of course, that is used up by the extra cost of building in the wintertime.

One hon. member referred to the fact the government had made certain amendments to the National Housing Act in order to lower interest rates and extend the period of amortization. I would suggest that this is not going to solve the problem or meet the need. It may be a matter of putting a little money into one pocket and taking it out of the other, but it will not accomplish anything so far as the potential home owner is concerned.
Even those who are remodelling or repairing their present homes will be affected. I had a letter from one of them who said he could not proceed to do necessary renovations to his home because of the imposition of this tax.
Mr. Chairman, there is an industry to which not too much reference has been made in this debate, and which is subject to this tax. I have here a telegram from Mr. L. P. Starck, of the Giant Mascot Mines Ltd. at Hope, British Columbia, and I want to read part of it as it points out something that has not been referred to in the course of this debate. It reads:
As western Canada's only nickel mine we wish to protest the imposition of 11 per cent tax on equipment and supplies used in manufacturing. Pyramiding effect of tax through all levels of manufacturing will ultimately increase material cost by some 15 to 18 per cent. This conservatively means cost increase to our company of $9,000 per month. Due to low prices and lack of markets in Canada we must sell our production to Japan on a long term fixed price contract without escalator clauses for increased cost. As we cannot pass increased cost on to consumer we must effect them by reducing crews and curtailing development and exploration projects. This means reduced employment. Ultimately this could result in closure of operation which would mean the loss of 150 jobs and a payroll of $80,000 per month in Hope.
As I say, that is just part of the telegram, and it asks for the repeal of this resolution.
Reference has been made to its effect on the entire construction industry, but I believe it will have a very detrimental effect right through our whole economy. We appreciate some of the changes that have been made since the introduction of the original resolution, and we appreciate the exemptions that are being continued. They will be of real importance in British Columbia. There has been some discussion tonight about universities and colleges, and in British Columbia plans are already under way for the erection of additional universities. This exemption will be of real benefit to such projects.
We also appreciate the exemptions now being provided to various municipalities, and are appreciative of the fact that the minister has indicated the imposition of the tax will be phased, with 4 per cent this year, another 4 per cent next spring and the remainder at the end of December 1964. However, even though this is appreciated, I do not think it is
Excise Tax Act
going to meet or answer the need of industry across the country. It is rather like the fellow who is going to cut his dog's tail off and he decides he will cut it off in little pieces because it would not hurt so much. That is the same principle which the minister is applying, to accomplish the same objectives in the final analysis.
Once again I would urge the minister to look at this situation and see if he could not discover some other more satisfactory way of obtaining the necessary revenue than by the imposition of a tax of this nature. I would remind him of the suggestions made by my colleague, the hon. member for Medicine Hat, and I ask him to give these careful consideration because they would be an effective alternative to the proposal now before us.
Mr. Chairman, would I be out of order if I suggested that we call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think you had better go ahead.

Under ordinary circumstances, even an opposition member might be expected to congratulate a minister of finance upon the presentation of one of his first submissions to the house. As the member for London, and anticipating an opportunity to participate in this discussion of the II per cent tax, I considered this an ordinary and a proper courtesy; but after due consideration I have come to the conclusion that neither proprieties of the house nor the dictates of common courtesy impose any such obligation.
Mr. Chairman, speaking on this resolution, let us not delude ourselves. This is still an 11 per cent tax, an escalator tax and, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings suggested some time ago, it is a tax that is a part of a budget of deceit and deception, of fiction and of fraud.
The Prime Minister once had an enviable reputation as minister of external affairs, as a diplomat, and as a Canadian. I was prepared to accord him every respect in his office of Prime Minister. This is only as it should be, regardless of what I might consider the inaccuracies and fallacies of the right hon. gentleman before and during the recent election campaign; but the Prime Minister must share with his Minister of Finance responsibility for the budget in all its details, including this 11 per cent escalator tax. The office of Prime Minister is now to be equated with the ineptness of the Minister of Finance.
For the average Canadian this tax is one part of a budget of disreputable gimmicks, even as the Liberal campaign in the last election was a campaign of phoney truth squads

Excise Tax Act
and colouring books. The committee is being asked to vote confidence in the government by giving its approval to this resolution. But, sir, it is a tax in which the government itself is already beginning to show signs of no confidence.
From individual builders, construction groups and manufacturing concerns all across the country, there has come a tide of protest against the imposition of this tax on building materials and production machinery. If one were to take the file of letters, telegrams and submissions that I have in my office, and multiply them by the 265 members in the Commons, it would represent an amazing array of protest and indignation.
This is the strangest of all the manoeuvres of the minister and his three budgeteers. The government wants to get the economy rolling; it wants to stimulate construction and increase employment. Yet it imposes an 11 per cent penalty upon business expansion in the form of new plant facilities. To help still further to increase employment and stimulate production, it slaps a similar tax on the very tools of industry, new production machinery and equipment.
I recently had a delegation from London, from an automobile firm which was contemplating a $21 million expansion program. They had already drawn plans for the building, but since then have cancelled the whole plan and are going to make automobile parts in an American plant and bring them in duty free-which they are able to do, and of course at a lower price than they can make them in Canada. All this is as a result of this prohibitive tax. That is only one item. Multiply it again by 265 ridings across the Dominion of Canada and immediately we have a loss of well over half a billion dollars, to say nothing of the loss of potential work for many thousands of people for years to come. I submit that this is a gigantic retrograde step.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Port Arthur mentioned public libraries. I raised this matter in the house at one time. I learned something on that occasion. All hon. members learn as they go along, or hope they will. I have received representations from the Canadian library association and from the London library, the main library in my constituency. May I refer to paragraph 4 of the resolution which refers to "a school, university or other similar educational institution". I am wondering just how similar it has to be, and just how more similar an institution that supplies learning for people from the time they go to kindergarten until they go to the grave could be to a school,

university or other similar educational institution. I have no doubt that the minister thinks he knows all the answers, but there is an old saying that goes something like this: "When you review the things you think you know, you get to know the things you thought you knew".
Across the country business and industry contemplating new plant and equipment will start to prune and trim capital outlays. The deeper and more drastic the pruning, the less will be the minister's estimated revenue flow from that source. More important, millions of dollars in orders for materials, machinery and equipment will be cut back. With these cut-backs will be applied the brake to supplying industries and providing employment. Just as in the case I have cited with regard to the automobile supply firm, Eaton Automotive Company of London, I can only regard this as one of the most disastrous decisions taken by this government within its vaunted 60 days of decision. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is a vicious and unwarranted tax brought to bear upon one of the most sensitive sectors of our economy. It is a reprehensible tax imposed by a discredited minister and a discredited government. In the best interests-
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member what is discreditable about placing equipment supplies and construction material industries in precisely the same position as other industries?
Put it on the order paper.

Mr. Chairman, there are people who have sat in this house for so long they have become benevolent in their thinking. I do not exactly know what the hon. member said because he was not very clear. But I will talk to him again some other time. I was just saying that in the best interests of the country and the government itself, the Minister of Finance should withdraw this tax or resign forthwith.
Hear, hear.

Nothing he can now say or do will ever restore confidence in him as a finance minister in the tradition of Canada and the Canadian parliament. Mr. Chairman, when this tax was introduced the minister, with that brand of narrow partisanship with which he has so characterized himself, trumpeted that the brain truster would seek out any and all skeletons from the Conservative fiscal closet. It seems to me that the minister himself is the one that is haunted; he is haunted now by the spectres of the three

hired budgeteers, the clatter of the ticker-tape machines making fortunes for the big speculators as a consequence of his ignorance and thoughtlessness. It is the minister who is harried by thoughts of what may next plop out of the Liberal closet of ineptitude and gimmickry. Mr. Chairman, Britain has its Profumo case. Canada has its "perfumo" case, in this whole tragic and demoralizing episode of an excuse for a budget. In short, sir, this is part of a tainted budget contrived by a discredited minister and a government in bad odour.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock?
No.

Argue the point now. Keep it going until ten o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, upon rising to make a few remarks on the resolution now before us, I cannot help taking this opportunity to recall the election campaigns of 1962 and 1963 and to compare them with what happened on the eve of June 13, 1963.
If you remember, Mr. Chairman, during both last election campaigns, the team now sitting on the treasury benches had led the population of Canada to believe that a Liberal administration would cure all ills and that its coming into office would change Canada in such a way that it would become a new Eden.
However, the people were bitterly disappointed when they learned, since June 13 last, what the Liberal team was up to.
Budget night was remarkable in its own way for the people of Canada, because it gave birth to dissatisfaction and doubt about the economic future of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that it is now ten o'clock?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would hope that tomorrow we would complete the resolution, so we could then proceed. If we do complete it before the end of the day tomorrow, we would ask to have first reading of the bill based upon it.
